Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 1–2:

(p-5) Surat al-A'raf is Meccan, except for eight verses from His saying ﴿Ask them﴾ up to His saying ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them﴾. All of it is muhkam (decisive, clear in meaning). It is said that the exception is only His exalted saying ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾. Its verses number two hundred and five or six.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad.﴾ The discussion of its like has already preceded.

﴿A Book﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a Book; or it is the predicate of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad﴾, and what is meant by it is the surah or the Qur'an. ﴿Sent down to you﴾ is its attribute. ﴿So let there be no constriction in your breast because of it﴾ means doubt, for the doubter has a constricted breast, or a tight heart, out of conveying it, for fear that you will be denied in it, or that you will fall short in discharging its right. The directing of the prohibition at him is for emphasis, like their saying: "Let me not see you here." The fa' may be conjunctive or consequential, so it is as if it were said: when it has been sent down to you so that you may warn by it, let your breast not be constricted. ﴿That you may warn by it﴾ is connected either to ﴿sent down﴾ or to ﴿let there be no constriction﴾, because when he is certain that it is from Allah, he becomes bold in warning, and likewise when he does not fear them, or when he knows that he is granted success in standing up to conveying it.

﴿And a reminder for the believers﴾ may be in the accusative, with its verb omitted, meaning: that you may warn by it and remind, a reminder, since it carries the sense of admonition; or in the genitive, as a conjunction with the place of ﴿that you may warn﴾; or in the nominative, as a conjunction with ﴿A Book﴾ or as the predicate of the omitted subject.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 3:

﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ encompasses the Qur'an and the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition), by His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾. ﴿And do not follow, other than Him, allies﴾ who would mislead you, from among the jinn and mankind. It has been said that the pronoun in ﴿other than Him﴾ refers back to ﴿what has been sent down﴾, meaning: and do not follow, other than the religion of God, allies. It has also been read as «ولا تَبْتَغُوا» (wa-la tabtaghu, "and do not seek"). ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, meaning a little remembrance, or a little time you remember, in that you abandon the religion of God and follow other than it. The «ما» (ma) is superfluous, for emphasis of the paucity; and if it is made a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), then ﴿qalilan﴾ ("little") is not governed by ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ ("you remember"). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ with the letter ta' elided, and Ibn ʿAmir read «يَتَذَكَّرُونَ» (yatadhakkarun), on the basis that the address thereafter is still with the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And how many a town We have destroyed!﴾ (many towns, i.e. many of the cities). ﴿We destroyed it﴾: We intended to destroy its people, or: We destroyed it by abandonment (al-khidhlan, i.e. withdrawal of divine support). ﴿Then Our punishment came upon it﴾: its people came, i.e. Our punishment (ba's, "might," here meaning Our chastisement) came upon it. ﴿By night﴾: while they were spending the night, like the people of Lot; baytan is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). ﴿Or while they were resting at midday﴾: it is coordinated with what precedes, meaning: resting at midday, like the people of Shu'ayb. The circumstantial waw has been omitted because of the heaviness of two coordinating particles coming together; it is a waw of coordination that has been borrowed for connection, not a substitute for a pronoun, since that would not be eloquent. In both expressions there is an intensification of their heedlessness and their sense of security from the punishment; for this reason the two times were specified, and because they are times of ease and rest, so that the coming of punishment during them is more dreadful.

﴿So their cry was not, when Our punishment came upon them, except that they said: Indeed we were wrongdoers﴾: "their cry" means their supplication and appeal for help, or what they used to claim of their religion. ﴿Except that they said...﴾: except their acknowledgment of their wrongdoing in what they were upon, and its falsehood, out of regret over themselves.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 6–7:

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, concerning their acceptance of the message and their response to the messengers. ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾, concerning what they were answered with. The purpose of this questioning is to rebuke and reprimand the disbelievers. The questioning negated in His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ is the questioning of inquiry (istilam, seeking information). Or the first is at the station of reckoning, and this one is at the time they incur the punishment.

﴿Then We will surely relate to them﴾, to the messengers, when they say ﴿We have no knowledge; surely You are the Knower of the unseen﴾, or to the messengers and those to whom they were sent, what they used to do. ﴿With knowledge﴾, being knowers of their outward and inward states, or with Our knowledge of them. ﴿And We were not absent﴾ from them, so that anything of their circumstances would be hidden from Us.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 7, verses 8–9:**

﴿And the weighing﴾ means the judgment, or the weighing of deeds, which is setting them against their recompense. The majority (al-Jumhur) of scholars hold that the records of deeds are weighed on a scale (mizan) that has a pointer (lisan) and two pans, which all creation looks at, to show justice (al-mu'daladah) and to cut off excuses. Just as He questions them about their deeds, their tongues will confess to them and their limbs will bear witness against them. This is supported by what is related: a man will be brought to the scale, and ninety-nine registers (sijill) will be unrolled for him, each register extending as far as the eye can see. Then a card (bitaqah) will come out for him, containing the two testimonies of faith (kalimatا al-shahadah). The registers will be placed in one pan and the card in the other, and the registers will be outweighed while the card is heavier.

It is also said that persons themselves are weighed, based on what is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A great, fat man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and he will not weigh before Allah the wing of a mosquito."

﴿On that day﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is "the weighing."

﴿The truth﴾ is its attribute (sifah), or it is a omitted predicate, and its meaning is the upright justice.

﴿Then as for him whose scales are heavy﴾ means his good deeds, or what his good deeds are weighed with. Thus it is the plural of mawzun (the weighed thing) or of mizan (scale), and its plural form is due to the variety of things weighed and the multiplicity of weighings.

﴿Those are the successful﴾ who are triumphant with salvation and reward.

﴿And as for him whose scales are light, those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾ by squandering the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which they were created, and by committing what exposed them to punishment.

﴿Because they used to wrong Our signs﴾ by denying them instead of affirming them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 10–11:

﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We enabled you to dwell in it, to cultivate it, and to dispose of it. ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood﴾, meaning: causes by which you live, the plural of maʿīshah (livelihood). It is related from Nafiʿ that he read it with a hamzah (maʿāyiʾ), by analogy with what has an extra yāʾ in it, like ṣaḥāʾif (pages). ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾, for what We have bestowed upon you.

﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you﴾, meaning: We created your father Adam from clay, not yet fashioned, then We fashioned him. The creation and fashioning of him is treated as the creation and fashioning of all of you, or it means: We began your creation, then your fashioning, in that We created Adam and then fashioned him. ﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate yourselves before Adam"﴾. It has been said that "then" (thumma) indicates the delay of the report. ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾, meaning: among those who prostrated to Adam.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 12–13:

﴿He said: "Then go down from it."﴾ From the heaven or from the Garden (al-Jannah). ﴿It is not for you﴾ meaning: it is not proper for you ﴿to be arrogant therein﴾ and disobedient, for it is the place of the humble (al-khashi') and the obedient (al-muti'). In this there is an admonition that arrogance does not befit the people of the Garden, and that He, glorified and exalted, only expelled him and sent him down because of his arrogance, not merely because of his disobedience. ﴿So get out, for you are among the debased﴾ among those whom Allah has humiliated because of his arrogance. The prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "Whoever humbles himself, Allah raises him, and whoever is arrogant, Allah lowers him."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 14–15:

﴿He said: "Reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ Grant me respite until the Day of Resurrection, so that I do not die, or do not hasten my punishment.

﴿He said: "Indeed, you are among those reprieved."﴾ Outwardly this requires that his request be granted, but it is to be understood in light of what came restricted by His words: ﴿until the Day of the appointed time﴾, which is the first blast (of the Trumpet), or a time at which Allah knows the end of his term to be. In His granting him this respite lies a trial for the servants and an exposure of them to reward through their opposing him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 16–17:

﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray"﴾ That is, after You have granted me respite, "I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path" by whatever means I can, because of Your leading me astray, through them, by way of designation (tasmiyah), or by way of driving (them) to error (hamlan ʿala al-ghayy), or by way of imposing upon them that for which I went astray. The bāʾ (because) is connected to the omitted verb of oath, not to "I will surely lie in wait," for the lām (of the oath) prevents it from governing what precedes it. It was also said that the bāʾ is for the oath: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾ watching over them, as highwaymen sit in wait for travellers, ﴿on Your straight path﴾, the path of Islam. He put it in the accusative as an adverb of place, as in his saying:

﴿A spear, swayed by the hand, whose shaft slides through it / as the fox slides along the road.﴾

It was also said that the estimated sense is "upon Your straight path," as in their saying: "Zayd struck the back and the belly."

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾ That is, from all four directions.

He likened his intention towards them, through beautification and misguidance, from whatever direction he can, to an enemy coming at them from the four directions. For this reason he did not say "from above them" or "from beneath their feet." It was also said that he did not say "from above them" because mercy descends from Him, and he did not say "from beneath them" because coming from below would frighten people. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "from before them" means from the side of the Hereafter, "from behind them" from the side of this world, and "from their right and from their left" from the direction of their good deeds and their bad deeds. It may also be said: "from before them" refers to what they know and are able to guard against; "from behind them" refers to what they do not know and are not able to (guard against); "from their right and from their left" refers to what it is easy for them to know and to guard against, but they did not do so because of their lack of vigilance and caution. The verb was made to govern the first two with the preposition of origin (min), since from those two directions it comes toward them, and the last two with the preposition of passing beyond (ʿan), since the one who comes from those two sides is like one who deviates from them and passes by their flank; a parallel to this is the saying "I sat to his right" (jalastu ʿan yamīnihi).

﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ that is, obedient. He said this as a conjecture based on the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾, when he saw among them many sources of evil and one source of good. It was also said that he heard it from the angels.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 18–19:

﴿He said: "Go forth from it, disgraced and expelled."﴾ "Madhw'man" (disgraced) is from "dha'amahu," meaning he reproached him. It is also read "madhuman," like "masulun" in "masul," or like "makulun" in "makil," from "dhamma-hu" (he reproached him), yudhimuhu dhaymam. "Madhhuran" means expelled, driven away. ﴿Whoever follows you of them﴾: the lam in "liman" is the lam of preparation for an oath, and its answer is ﴿Surely I will fill Hell with you all﴾, which takes the place of the answer of the conditional. It is also read "liman" with a kasra on the lam, as the predicate of "la-amla'anna," meaning: this threat is for whoever follows you; or it is the cause of "uhrij" (go forth). "La-amla'anna" is the answer of an omitted oath. The meaning of ﴿of you﴾ is "of you" (addressing him) and "of them," so the addressee is given precedence.

﴿And O Adam﴾: that is, and We said, "O Adam." ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you become among the wrongdoers.﴾ It is also read "hadhi," which is the original form; its diminutive is "dhayya," and the ha' is a substitute for the ya'. ﴿Lest you become among the wrongdoers﴾: that is, lest you become among those who wronged themselves. "Takunama" may be jussive, by coordination, or subjunctive, as an answer.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 7, verse 20:**

﴿So Satan whispered to them.﴾ That is, he performed the *waswasa* (whispering) on their account. Originally *waswasa* means a faint sound, like the murmur or the rustle, and from it comes the expression *waswasa al-hilyu* (the ornament made a faint sound). Its manner has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. ﴿To reveal to them﴾ means to expose to them. The *lam* here is either the *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence) or the *lam al-gharad* (the lam of purpose). It is possible that he also intended, by his whispering, to distress them by exposing their private parts, and for this reason he referred to them as *sawʾah* (shame, i.e. what causes shame). This indicates that uncovering the *awrah* (private parts) in seclusion and in front of a spouse without need is ugly and repugnant to natural disposition.

﴿That which was concealed from them of their private parts.﴾ That is, what was covered from them of their *'awrat* (private parts). They did not see them in themselves, nor did one of them see the other's. The reason the *waw* with a *damma* was not changed into a *hamza* in the well-known reading, as it was in *Uwayṣil* (the diminutive of *Wasil*), is that the second [*waw*] is a *madda* (a long vowel). It was also read as *sawatihima*, with the *hamza* dropped and its vowel transferred onto the *waw*, and as *sawwatihima*, by changing the *hamza* into a *waw* and assimilating the quiescent *waw* into it.

﴿And he said: "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become two angels﴾ — that is, out of dislike that you become angels — ﴿or become among those who abide forever﴾, who do not die, or who remain forever in Paradise." It has been cited as evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. The answer to this is that it was known that realities do not change; rather, their desire was that there would also be attained for them what the angels have of innate perfections, and independence from food and drink. That does not indicate the angels' superiority absolutely.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 21–22:

It is said that they both swore to him by acceptance (al-qabul). It is also said that they both made him swear by Allah that he was indeed among the sincere advisors (al-nasihin), so he swore to them both, and this was made a mutual oath (muqasamah).

﴿So he led them down⌄﴾ He brought them down to eating from the tree. By this he indicates that He caused them to descend by this from a high rank to a low station, for al-tadliyah and al-idla' mean sending a thing from above to below. ﴿with deception⌄﴾ by what he deceived them with through the oath, for they thought that no one swears by Allah falsely; or they were entangled in deception. ﴿And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them⌄﴾ that is, when they found its taste and began eating from it, punishment and the ill effect of disobedience seized them, so their clothing fell away from them and their private parts (awrat) became visible to them.

It has been differed over whether the tree was the ear of grain, the vine, or something else, and whether the clothing was light, a garment, or fingernails. ﴿And they began⌄﴾ to patch (yakhsifan), that is, they began to mend and stick one leaf upon another. ﴿over themselves of the leaves of the Garden⌄﴾ It is said it was fig leaves. It was also read as "yakhsifan" from akhsafa, meaning they were covering themselves, and yakhsifan from khasafa, and yakhsifan, whose origin is yakhtasifan. ﴿And their Lord called out to them: Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is a clear enemy to you?⌄﴾ This is a rebuke for opposing the prohibition and a reproach for being deceived by the words of the enemy. It contains evidence that an absolute prohibition indicates prohibition (al-tahrim).

"They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers." — ﴿قالا رَبَّنا ظَلَمْنا أنْفُسَنا﴾ — we harmed them through disobedience and by exposing them to expulsion from the Garden. ﴿وَإنْ لَمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنا وتَرْحَمْنا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾ — this is evidence that minor sins (al-saghā'ir) are punishable if they are not forgiven. The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible to punish for them when major sins (al-kabā'ir) are avoided; and for this reason they said: they only said that out of the custom of those brought near (to God), in magnifying a small misdeed and belittling a great good deed.

﴿قالَ اهْبِطُوا﴾ — the address is to Adam, Eve and their offspring, or to the two of them and Iblis. He repeated the command to him (Iblis) as a follower, so that it would be known that they are enemies forever, and He related what He said to them separately. ﴿بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ — in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: hostile to one another. ﴿وَلَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾ — settlement (istiqrār), i.e., a place of settling. ﴿وَمَتاعٌ﴾ — and enjoyment (tamattu'). ﴿إلى حِينٍ﴾ — until your appointed terms (ājāl) are fulfilled.

"They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers." — ﴿قالا رَبَّنا ظَلَمْنا أنْفُسَنا﴾ — we harmed them through disobedience and by exposing them to expulsion from the Garden. ﴿وَإنْ لَمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنا وتَرْحَمْنا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾ — this is evidence that minor sins (al-saghā'ir) are punishable if they are not forgiven. He said, ﴿In it you will live, and in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾, for the recompense. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Dhakwan read ﴿وَمِنها تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ (*wa-minha tukhrajūna*, with the *ta'* of *tukhrajūna* vowelled with a *fatha*, passive form), and in Surah al-Zukhruf, ﴿كَذَلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ (*kadhalika tukhrajūna*) is read with a *fatha* on the *tā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*. (These are variant readings, *qira'at*, of the Qur'an.)

﴿O Children of Adam, We have indeed sent down to you clothing﴾, meaning We created it for you through heavenly arrangements and descending causes. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down for you eight kinds of livestock﴾, and His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾. ﴿It covers your private parts﴾, which Satan intended to expose, ﴿and it is an adornment﴾, sparing you from having to stitch leaves together.

It is narrated that the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, saying, "We will not circle the House in garments in which we have disobeyed God," so this was revealed.

Perhaps he mentioned the story of Adam as a preface to this, so as to make known that the exposure of nakedness was the first evil that Satan brought upon humanity, and that he misled them in this just as he misled their parents. ﴿And as plumage﴾, meaning clothing with which you beautify yourselves. *Al-rīsh* (plumage, finery) means beauty. It has been said that it means wealth, and from this comes *tarayyasha al-rajul* (the man became wealthy) when he acquired property. It is also read as *riyāshan*, which is the plural of *rīsh*, like *shu'ab* and *shi'āb*. ﴿And the garment of piety﴾ is the fear of God.

It has been said that it is faith. It has been said that it is good conduct. It has been said that it is the garment of war. It is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is: ﴿that is better﴾, or "better" is the predicate and "that" is its attribute, as if it were said: "And the garment of piety, the one referred to, is better." Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *wa-libāsa al-taqwā* in the accusative, coordinating it with *libāsan* (clothing). ﴿That﴾, meaning the sending down of clothing, ﴿is among the signs of God﴾, which indicate His grace and mercy, ﴿that perhaps they may remember﴾, so that they recognise His blessing, or ﴿take heed﴾ and thus refrain from vile deeds.

He said, ﴿In it you will live, and in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾, for the recompense. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Dhakwan read ﴿وَمِنها تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ (*wa-minha tukhrajūna*, with the *ta'* of *tukhrajūna* vowelled with a *fatha*, passive form), and in Surah al-Zukhruf, ﴿كَذَلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ (*kadhalika tukhrajūna*) is read with a *fatha* on the *tā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*. (These are variant readings, *qira'at*, of the Qur'an.)

O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you (fatnanna) as he expelled your two parents from the Garden, (lā yumḥinannakum, "let him not test you") by preventing you from entering the Garden through your misguiding you. ﴿As he expelled your two parents from the Garden⦆ as he tested your two parents by expelling them from it. The prohibition is in wording directed at Satan, while the meaning is their prohibition from following him and being seduced by him. ﴿Stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾ is a circumstantial clause, either from "your two parents" or from the subject of "expelled"; the attribution of the stripping to him is causal. ﴿Indeed he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them﴾ is a reason for the prohibition and an emphasis on the warning against his temptation. ﴿And his tribe﴾ means his troops. Their seeing us from where we do not see them, in general, does not preclude their being seen by us or their taking on forms before us. ﴿Indeed We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾ by what We have placed between them of affinity, or by sending them upon them, empowering them to forsake them, and driving them to what they have made attractive to them. This verse is the purpose of the story and the summation of the narrative.

﴿And when they commit an immoral act﴾: an act at the extreme of ugliness, such as worshipping an idol and uncovering the private parts during circumambulation (ṭawāf). ﴿They say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to do it."﴾ They offered an excuse and argued with two claims: imitation of the forefathers (taqlīd, blind following of ancestors), and attributing a falsehood to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. He set aside the first, because its corruption is evident, and refuted the second with His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality."﴾ This is because the custom of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is to command good deeds and to urge noble character. This verse does not indicate that the ugliness of an act, in the sense that blame for it follows in the Hereafter, is known by reason (ʿaqlī). Rather, what is meant by immoral act (fāḥisha) is that which a sound nature recoils from and which upright reason regards as deficient. It has also been said that the two statements are answers to two sequential questions, as if it were said to them when they had done it: "Why did you do it?" They said: "We found our fathers doing it." It was then said: "From where did your fathers take it?" They said: "Allah commanded us to do it." On both interpretations, imitation is prohibited when evidence to the contrary has been established, not absolutely. ﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ This is a rebuke that implies a prohibition against attributing falsehood to Allah, exalted is He.

Say: My Lord has commanded justice (al-qist), that is, with equity (al-'adl), which is the middle course in every matter, keeping away from both extremes of excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit).

﴿And set your faces [upright]﴾: direct yourselves toward His worship, upright, not turning aside to other than Him; or, set them toward the qiblah. ﴿At every place of prostration﴾: at every time of prostration or its place, which is prayer; or in any mosque where the prayer has come upon you, and do not delay it until you return to your mosques. ﴿And call upon Him﴾: worship Him. ﴿Sincere to Him in religion﴾: that is, in obedience, for to Him is your return. ﴿As He originated you﴾: as He brought you into being at first. ﴿You will return﴾: by His restoring you, so He will recompense you for your deeds; so devote your worship sincerely to Him. He compared the restoration to the origination only to establish that it is possible and that He is able to do it. It has also been said: as He originated you from dust, you will return to it. It has also been said: as He originated you barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, you will return. It has also been said: as He originated you as believers and disbelievers, He will restore you.

﴿A party He guided﴾: by enabling them to believe. ﴿And a party upon whom error was made due﴾: in accordance with the prior decree. Its grammatical position is governed by a verb implied by what follows it, i.e., "and He forsook a party." ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah﴾: this gives the reason for their being forsaken, or confirms their error. ﴿And they think that they are guided﴾: this indicates that the disbelieving one who errs and the one who is stubbornly obstinate are equal in deserving blame; and the difference is that one may attribute it to the one who fails to examine (the matter) carefully.

Its grammatical position is governed by a verb implied by what follows it, i.e., "and He forsook a party." ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah﴾: this gives the reason for their being forsaken, or confirms their error. ﴿And they think that they are guided﴾: this indicates that the disbelieving one who errs and the one who is stubbornly obstinate are equal in deserving blame; and the difference is that one may attribute it to the one who fails to examine (the matter) carefully.

O Children of Adam, take your adornment (i.e., your clothes) to cover your nakedness, at every place of worship (for circumambulation or prayer). It is part of the Sunnah that a man take the best appearance for prayer, and in this is evidence for the obligation of covering the nakedness in prayer. And eat and drink, (of) what is good for you.

It is narrated that the Banu Amir, during their pilgrimage days, would not eat anything except staple food, and would not eat fat, thereby glorifying their pilgrimage; so they were made Muslims by this, and the verse was revealed.

And do not be extravagant (by prohibiting what is lawful, or by transgressing into what is unlawful, or by excess in food and gluttony over it). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Eat what you wish and wear what you wish, so long as two things do not touch you: extravagance and arrogance." And 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid said: "Allah has gathered medicine (the art of healing) into half a verse: (Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant)." Indeed, He does not love the extravagant, i.e., He does not approve of their conduct.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 32:

﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ [that is, of clothing and all other things by which one beautifies oneself], ﴿which He has brought forth for His servants﴾ [from plants, such as cotton and flax; from animals, such as silk and wool; and from minerals, such as coats of mail], ﴿and the good things of provision﴾ [the pleasant foods and drinks]. In this is evidence that the basic ruling concerning foods, clothing, and all kinds of adornment is permissibility (ibahah), because the interrogative in "Who" (man) is for denunciation (inkar). ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾ [primarily], while the disbelievers, although they share in them, do so only secondarily (tab'). ﴿Purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [no one else shares in them], and its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Nafi' read it in the nominative, making it a second predicate (khabar ba'da khabar). ﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who know﴾ [meaning: just as We have detailed this ruling, We detail all the other rulings for them].

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 33–34:

﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾: the ones whose ugliness increases. It has also been said: what pertains to the private parts. ﴿What is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾: their open and their secret forms. ﴿And sin﴾: and what necessitates sin. This is generalization after specification. It has also been said: drinking wine. ﴿And transgression﴾: injustice, or arrogance; he singled it out for mention for emphasis. ﴿Without right﴾: this is connected to "transgression" and, in meaning, reinforces it. ﴿And that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾: a mockery of the polytheists, and an alert to the prohibition of following what no proof attests to. ﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾: by deviating from the truth regarding His attributes, glory be to Him and exalted, and by fabricating against Him, such as their saying ﴿God has commanded us to do it﴾.

﴿For every community there is a term﴾: a period, or a time for the descent of punishment upon them; this is a warning to the people of Mecca. ﴿So when their term comes﴾: their period has run its course, or their time has arrived. ﴿They will not delay it an hour, nor will they hasten it﴾: that is, they will not be late or early by the briefest span of time; or they will not seek to postpone or advance it, because of the intensity of the terror.

﴿And those who deny Our signs and turn away from them in arrogance — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ The meaning is: whoever of you guards against denial and sets right his deeds, and those of you who deny Our signs. The placing of the *fa'* (الفاء) in the first predicate (الخبر, the predicate) but not in the second is for emphasis in the promise and for leniency in the threat.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 37:

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾ (That is,) one who attributes to Allah what He has not said, or denies what He has said.

﴿Those will receive their portion from the Book﴾ — of what has been decreed for them of provisions and terms of life. It has also been said that "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), meaning: of what has been recorded for them in it. ﴿Until, when Our messengers come to them, taking their souls﴾ — i.e., taking their souls (arwah), and this is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the messengers. "Until" (hatta) marks the endpoint (ghayah) of their receiving their portion, and it is the particle after which speech begins anew. ﴿They say﴾ — this is the response (jawab) of "when." ﴿Where is what you used to call upon besides Allah?﴾ — i.e., where are the deities you used to worship? The word "ma" is joined to "ayna" in the script of the Mushaf, though by rule it should be separated, since it is a relative (mawsulah). ﴿They will say: They have vanished from us﴾ — they have disappeared from us. ﴿And they will bear witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ — they acknowledged that they had been astray in what they were upon.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 7, verses 38–39:**

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 40–41:

﴿And they will not enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.﴾ That is, until something similar in bulk to the body, namely the camel, enters what is similar in narrowness of passage, namely the hole of a needle. And that does not happen; so what depends on it likewise does not happen. The word "al-jamal" (camel) has also been read as "al-qamal" (louse), "al-jumal" as "al-nughar" (a type of small bird's sound pattern; here the vowel pattern of "nughar"), "al-juml" as "al-qufl" (lock), "al-jumul" as "al-nusub" (idols/stone markers), and "al-jamal" as "al-habl" (rope), which is a thick rope made of hemp; and it is said it is the rope of a ship. "Samm" may be pronounced with a damma or a kasra, and "summ" (with damma) for the eye of a needle. "Al-khiyat" is what is sewn with, such as a belt or a strap. ﴿And thus﴾ and like that terrible recompense, ﴿We recompense the criminals.﴾

﴿For them there will be a bed of Hell﴾, a spread. ﴿And above them canopies﴾, coverings. The tanwin in "ghawashin" is, according to Sibawayh, a substitute for the elided letter, and according to others it is the tanwin of declension (sarf). It has also been read as "ghawasi" by dropping the elided element. ﴿And thus We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ He described them as "criminals" at one point and as "wrongdoers" at another, indicating that by their denial of the verses they were characterized by these blameworthy attributes; and He mentioned crime together with deprivation from Paradise, and wrongdoing together with punishment by the Fire, as an alert that it is the greatest of crimes.

On His customary practice, glorified and exalted is He, of coupling the threat with the promise, comes ﴿And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity; those are the companions of the Garden; they will abide therein forever﴾. The clause ﴿And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical insertion, placed between a subject and its predicate), made to encourage the acquisition of everlasting bliss through what people's power can bear and what is easy for them. It is also read as ﴿لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ﴾ (*lā tukallafu nafsun*, with the verb in the passive).

﴿And We will remove whatever rancour is in their breasts﴾, meaning: We will remove from their hearts the causes of rancour, or We will purify their hearts of it, so that among them there will be nothing but mutual affection.

It is related from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face: "I truly hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah and al-Zubayr will be among them."

﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾, as an addition to their delight and joy. ﴿And they will say: "Praise belongs to God, who guided us to this"﴾, that is, to that for which this is the reward. ﴿We would not have been guided had God not guided us﴾, that is, had there been no guidance from God and His enabling grace. The *lām* (in *lanahtadiya*) is for emphasizing the negation, and the response to *lawlā* (had it not been for) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it.

Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿مَا كُنَّا﴾ (*mā kunnā*) without the *wāw*, making this clause explanatory of the first. ﴿Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾, so we were guided through their guidance.

They say this out of exultation and gladness, because what they knew with certainty (*ʿilm al-yaqīn*) in this world has become for them the certainty of sight (*ʿayn al-yaqīn*) in the Hereafter. ﴿And they will be called: "That is the Garden, which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do"﴾. This may be when they see it from afar, or after entering it, and the one calling out is God Himself. ﴿You have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾, that is, it has been given to you because of your deeds. This phrase is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) relating to *al-Janna* (the Garden), with the governing element being the sense of indication (*ishārah*) in *tilkum*; or it is a predicate, with *al-Janna* being an adjective of *tilkum*. The *anna* in the five positions is either the light (*mukhaffafah*) form or the explanatory (*mufassirah*) form, because the calling out and the proclamation are a kind of speech.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 44–45:

(p-14) ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire: "We have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you too found what your Lord promised to be true?"﴾ They said this only to boast of their own state, to gloat over the companions of the Fire, and to cause them grief. And the reason He did not say "what He promised you," as He said "what He promised us," is that what displeased them of what was promised was not, in its entirety, specifically promised to them, such as the Resurrection, the Reckoning, and the bounties of the people of the Garden. ﴿They said, "Yes."﴾ Al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿimm, "Yes" as ʿim), and both are dialects. ﴿Then a caller will call out between them﴾: it was said that he is the one who holds the Trumpet (ṣāḥib al-ṣuwar). ﴿between them﴾: between the two groups.

﴿That the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn Kathir, in the narration of al-Bazzi, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿that the curse of Allah﴾ with tashdid (emphatic doubling) and nasb (accusative). It has also been read as ﴿inna﴾ with a kasra, either on the intention of saying, or by treating ʾadhdhana (announced) as qāla (said).

﴿Those who bar from the way of Allah﴾: an attributive adjective (ṣifah) of "the wrongdoers" that confirms their description, or a dhamm (censure) in the nominative or accusative. ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾: deviation and inclination away from what it is. Al-iwaj with a kasra, in meanings and in visible things, is what is not upright; with a fatḥa, it is what is in an upright thing, such as a wall or a spear. ﴿And they are, of the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 7, verses 46–47:**

﴿And between them is a barrier﴾, i.e., between the two groups, in line with His saying, ﴿So a wall will be set up between them﴾ (57:13). Or it is between Paradise and Hellfire, to prevent the effect of each from reaching the other.

﴿And on the A'raf﴾ (*al-A'raf*, the heights), i.e., on the heights of the barrier, which is the wall set up between them. *A'raf* is the plural of *'urf*, a term borrowed from the *'urf* (mane) of a horse. It was also said that *'urf* refers to whatever is elevated from a thing, since it is more recognizable than others due to its prominence.

﴿Men﴾: a group of *muwahhidun* (*muwahhidun*, those who affirm God's oneness) who fell short in their deeds, and so they are held back between Paradise and Hellfire until God, glorified and exalted is He, decides concerning them what He wills. It was also said that they are a people whose ranks are elevated, such as the prophets, peace be upon them, or the martyrs, may God be pleased with them, or the best of the believers and their scholars, or angels who appear in the form of men.

﴿They will recognize each [group]﴾, i.e., of the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire, ﴿by their mark﴾, by their sign which God has informed them of, such as the whiteness and blackness of the faces. *Sīmā* is on the pattern *fa'ala* (*fa'ala*, a morphological form) from *sāma* (to pasture), as in *sāma ibilahu* (he let his camels graze, marked as such), or from *wasama* (to mark), as in the mark on the forehead. They recognize this only through inspiration (*ilham*) or through the teaching of the angels.

﴿And they will call out to the companions of Paradise: "Peace be upon you."﴾ That is, when they look at them, they greet them with peace. ﴿They have not entered it, but they aspire [to]﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the *waw* (the plural pronoun) according to the first interpretation, and from *ashab* (companions) according to the remaining interpretations.

﴿And when their sights are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ That is, in the Fire. (They say) "We seek refuge in God."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 48–49:

﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks﴾ from among the leaders of the disbelievers. ﴿They will say: "Of no avail to you was your multitude (jam'ukum)"﴾, meaning your number (kathratukum), or your gathering of wealth (jam'ukum al-mal). ﴿"And your arrogance (wa ma kuntum tastakbirun)"﴾ against the truth, or against creation. It has also been read as "tastakthirun" (you were profuse), from al-kathrah (abundance).

﴿"Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy?"﴾ This is a continuation of their words to the men. The reference is to the weak people of Paradise, whom the disbelievers used to despise in the world and swear that Allah would not admit them to Paradise. ﴿"Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve."﴾ That is, they turned toward the people of Paradise and said to them, "Enter." This is more fitting with the last interpretations. Or it is said to the companions of the Heights: "Enter Paradise by the grace of Allah, glorified and exalted is He," after they had been detained until they saw both groups and recognized them, and spoke to them with what they spoke. It is said that when the people of the Fire taunted the companions of the Heights, the latter swore that the companions of the Heights would not enter Paradise, so Allah, glorified and exalted is He, or some of the angels, said: "Are these the ones of whom you swore..." It has also been read as "udkhilu" (enter, passive) and "dakhalu" (they entered), as a resumed statement, its implied sense being: they entered Paradise, being told: ﴿"No fear shall be upon you."﴾

﴿And the companions of the Fire call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour out on us some of the water"﴾, i.e., pour it (ṣubbūhu). This is evidence that the Garden is above the Fire. ﴿Or of what God has provided you﴾, from the rest of the drinks, so that it fits with "pour out"; or from the food, as in his saying: "I fed her straw and cold water." ﴿They will say: God has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾, He withheld them from them, the withholding of what is forbidden from one who is obligated.

﴿Those who took their religion as a diversion and a game﴾, like the forbidding of the baḥīrah (a she-camel whose ears were slit and released), the taṣdiyah (clapping as a form of worship) and the mukā' (whistling) around the House. Diversion (lahw) is diverting one's concern with what it is not good to divert it with, and play (la'ib) is seeking joy with what it is not good to seek joy with. ﴿And the life of this world deceived them. So today We will forget them﴾, We will treat them as those who forget, and so We will leave them in the Fire. ﴿As they forgot the meeting of this their Day﴾, so that they did not bring it to mind and did not prepare for it. ﴿And they used to deny Our signs﴾, and as they were deniers that they were from God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 52–53:

﴿And indeed, We brought them a Book which We had detailed﴾: We made its meanings clear, in detail, concerning the beliefs, the rulings and the admonitions. ﴿With knowledge﴾: knowing the manner of its detailing, until it came as wise (ḥakīm). In this there is evidence that He, glorified and exalted, is knowing with a knowledge (ʿālim bi-ʿilm), or comprising knowledge (mushtamilan ʿalā ʿilm), in which case it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the object (al-mafʿūl). It has also been read as "faḍḍalnāh" (We preferred it), meaning over all the other Books, knowing that it is deserving of that. ﴿A guidance and a mercy for a people who believe﴾: a ḥāl from the hāʾ (the pronoun referring to the Book).

﴿Do they await﴾: yantaẓirūn (they wait). ﴿Except its ta'wīl (final outcome)﴾: except what its matter will come to (yaʾūlu ilayhi amruhu), namely the clarification of its truthfulness through the manifestation of what it spoke of regarding promise and threat. ﴿On the day its ta'wīl comes, those who had forgotten it before will say﴾: they had abandoned it with the abandonment of one who forgets. ﴿The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth﴾: that is, it has become clear that they came with the truth. ﴿So have we any intercessors that they may intercede for us?﴾ today. ﴿Or are we to be returned﴾: or is it that we are returned to the world (al-dunyā)? It has also been read in the accusative (al-naṣb), as a conjunction upon "fa-yashfaʿū" (so that they intercede); or because "aw" here means "ilā an" (until). On the first reading, what is requested is one of the two matters: intercession, or their return to the world. On the second reading, they would have intercessors either for one of the two matters, or for a single matter, which is the return. ﴿So that we may do other than what we used to do﴾: this is the answer to the second interrogation. It has also been read in the nominative (al-rafʿ), meaning "fa-naḥnu naʿmalu" (so we do). ﴿They have lost themselves﴾: by spending their lives in disbelief. ﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾: it vanished from them, so it did not benefit them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 54:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ That is, in six periods of time, like His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ Or, in the measure of six days, for the day as commonly understood is the time from sunrise to sunset, and there was no such thing at that time. The creation of things gradually, although He is capable of bringing them into being at once, is a proof of choice (ikhtiyar), a lesson for the observers, and an exhortation to deliberation in affairs. ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ That is, His command was established, or He took dominion. From our companions (the Ash'aris), the istiwa' upon the Throne is an attribute of Allah without how (bila kayf), and the meaning is: He has an istiwa' upon the Throne in the manner He intends, exalted above settling and occupying a place. The Throne (al-'arsh) is the body that encompasses all other bodies, and it was so named for its elevation, or by way of likening it to the throne of kingship, since commands and arrangements descend from it. It was also said that it means dominion (al-mulk). ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ He veils it with it. He did not mention the reverse because it is known, or because the wording admits of both. For this reason it is read as ﴿yughshi al-layla al-nahara﴾ with the accusative on ﴿al-layla﴾ and the nominative on ﴿al-nahar﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read it with the doubled letter (tashdid) in this place and in "al-Ra'd," to indicate repetition. ﴿Seeking it urgently﴾ It follows it swiftly, as one who seeks it, with nothing separating the two. Al-hathith is an intensive form (fa'il) from al-hath (urging), and it is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a circumstantial state (hal) of the agent in the sense of "urging," or of the patient in the sense of "urged." ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾ by His decree and His direction. They are in the accusative by conjunction with "the heavens," and "subjected" (musakhkharat) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Ibn 'Amir read kulluha with the nominative, as a subject and predicate. ﴿Surely to Him belong the creation and the command﴾ for He is the Originator and the Disposer. ﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ exalted in His oneness in divinity, and magnified in His singularity in lordship.

The realization of the verse, and Allah the Glorious and Exalted knows best: the disbelievers were taking lords, so He made clear to them that the one deserving lordship is One, namely Allah the Glorious and Exalted, because to Him belong the creation and the command. He, glorified and exalted, created the world in a upright order and wise governance, so He originated the spheres, then adorned them with the stars, as He indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾. He then undertook the bringing into being of the lower bodies, creating a substance receptive to changing forms and differing configurations, then divided it into specific kinds of contrary effects and actions. He indicated this by His saying, ﴿and created the earth﴾, that is, what is in the direction of the bottom, in two days. Then He produced the three kinds of generated beings by composing their materials first and shaping them second, as He said after His saying ﴿created the earth in two days﴾: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days﴾, that is, together with the first two days, in accordance with His saying in Surah al-Sajdah: ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾. Then, when the world of dominion was complete for Him, He undertook its governance like a king seated on his throne to manage the kingdom. He arranged the affair from the heaven to the earth by moving the spheres, directing the stars, and alternating the nights and days. Then He stated explicitly what is the conclusion of the argument and its result, saying: ﴿Surely to Him belong the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Then He commanded them to call upon Him, humbly and sincerely, saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 55–56:

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.﴾ That is, [being] people of humility and secrecy, for concealment (ikhfa') is a sign of sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ Those who exceed what they were commanded in supplication and otherwise. By this he alerts that the one who supplicates should not ask for what is not befitting to him, such as the rank of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, or ascending to the heaven. It is also said that it refers to shouting in supplication and being verbose in it.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will be a people who will transgress in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: 'O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action.'" Then he recited: "Indeed, He does not love the transgressors."

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ through disbelief and sins, ﴿after its reformation﴾ through the sending of the prophets and the legislating of rulings. ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope.﴾ In a state of fear of rejection, due to the shortness of your hopes and your lack of deserving, and [in a state of] hope of His answering, out of grace and kindness, because of the abundance of His mercy. ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾ This gives preference to hope and alerts to what one may use as a means to obtain an answer. The word "near" (qarib) is in the masculine form: it may be because "mercy" is understood as "compassion" (rahim), or because it is an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e., "a near matter," or because it is patterned on fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, or because it is a verbal noun like "contradiction" (naqid), or because of the distinction between "near" in terms of kinship and "near" in other than kinship.(p-17)

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.﴾ That is, [being] people of humility and secrecy, for concealment (ikhfa') is a sign of sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ Those who exceed what they were commanded in supplication and otherwise. ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "الرِّيحَ" (al-rih, the wind) in the singular. ﴿as heralds﴾ (*nashran*) is the plural of *nushur*, in the sense of *nashir* (spreading). Ibn 'Amir read "نُشْرًا" (*nushran*) with a sukun on the shin wherever it occurs. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "نَشْرًا" (*nashran*) with a fatha on the nun wherever it occurs, as a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, a word describing the state of the subject), meaning "spreading" (*nashirat*), or as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), since sending and spreading are close in meaning. 'Asim read ﴿bushran﴾ (بُشْرًا), which is a lightened form of "بُشَّرٍ" (*bushsharin*), the plural of *bashir* (bearer of good news), and it has been read in that form. ﴿بُشْرًا﴾ with a fatha on the ba' is the verbal noun of "بَشَّرَهَ" (*bashsharahu*), meaning "bearing good tidings" (*bashirat*), or it means "glad tidings" (*bushra*).

﴿before His mercy﴾ means in front of His mercy, that is, the rain. The *saba* (east wind) stirs up the clouds, the *shamal* (north wind) gathers them, the *janub* (south wind) makes them pour forth, and the *dabur* (west wind) scatters them.

﴿until when they have borne﴾ means carried, and it is derived from *qillah* (lightness), because one who lifts a thing finds it light (*yastaqillu*).

﴿heavy clouds﴾ are heavy with water. He used the plural because "السَّحاب" (*al-sahab*, the clouds) is a collective noun meaning "السَّحائب" (*al-sahaib*, the clouds).

﴿We drove it﴾: that is, the clouds. The singular pronoun is used in view of the wording.

﴿to a dead land﴾: for its sake, or to give it life, or to water it. It has also been read "مَيْتٍ" (*mayt*).

﴿and We sent down water by it﴾: onto the land, or by means of the clouds, or by the driving, or by the wind, and likewise:

﴿and We brought forth by it﴾. It is possible that the pronoun here refers to ﴿the water﴾. If it refers to "البَلَد" (*al-balad*, the land), then the *ba'* in the first instance denotes attachment (*ilsaq*), and in the second it denotes location (*zarfiyyah*). If it refers to something else, then the *ba'* in both instances denotes causation (*sababiyyah*).

﴿of all kinds of fruits﴾: of all their types.

﴿Thus We bring forth the dead﴾: the reference here is either to the bringing forth of fruits, or to the giving of life to the dead land. That is, just as We give it life by producing the growing power within it and adorning it with kinds of plants and fruits, so We bring forth the dead from their graves and give them life by returning the souls to the substances of their bodies after gathering them and adorning them with powers and senses.

﴿so that you may remember﴾, and thus know that the One who is able to do that is able to do this.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ — the land that is good in soil (al-ard al-karimat al-turba).

﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ means by His will and facilitation. He expressed it this way to indicate the abundance, goodness and great benefit of the vegetation, because He placed it in contrast (muqabala).

﴿And that which is corrupt﴾ — i.e., like the harrah (rocky, lava-strewn land) and the sabakha (salt-flat).

﴿comes not forth except sparsely﴾ — meagre and of no benefit. Its being in the accusative (nasb) is as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the sense of the sentence is: "And the land that is corrupt, its vegetation comes forth only sparsely." The noun (muḍāf) was omitted and the noun it was attached to (muḍāf ilayh) was put in its place, so it became marfu' and concealed (mustatir). It has also been read as yukhriju, meaning the land brings it forth; then "illa nakidan" is the object (maf'ul). Nakidan is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "possessing meagreness." It has also been read as nakidan with sukun for lightening (takhfif).

﴿Thus do We vary the signs﴾ — We repeat them and reiterate them.

﴿for a people who give thanks﴾ — for God's blessing, so that they reflect upon it and take lessons from it. The verse is a parable for one who contemplates the signs and benefits from them, and for one who does not pay them any heed and is not affected by them.

The Quranic verse ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ is the answer (*jawab*) to an omitted oath (*qasam*). This lam is rarely used without *qad*, because it indicates expectation: when the addressee hears it, he expects the event it introduces to occur. Noah, son of Lamak, son of Mutawshalikh, son of Idris, was the first prophet after him. He was sent when he was fifty or forty years old. ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah"﴾, meaning worship Him alone, in accordance with His saying, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. Al-Kisa'i read «غَيْرِهِ» with a kasra, as a qualifier (*na't*) or substitute (*badal*) that follows the wording of the preceding word wherever it occurs, when the word before *ilah* is one of those that put the following noun in the genitive. It was also read with a fatha, as an exception (*istithna'*). ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ if you do not believe. This is a warning and an explanation of the call to worship Him. The day is the Day of Resurrection, or the day the flood descends.

﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾, meaning the nobles, for they fill the eyes with splendour. ﴿Indeed, we see you in error﴾, meaning departure from the truth.

(p-18)﴿clear﴾, meaning manifest.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 61–62:

﴿Qāla yā qawmi laysa bī ḍalālatun﴾ (He said: "O my people, there is no misguidance in me"), i.e., not any sort of ḍalāl (misguidance). He has gone to the extreme in negation, just as they went to the extreme in affirmation, and he alluded to them by it. ﴿Wa lākinnī rasūlun min rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾ (But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds) is an istidrāk (a corrective qualification) with regard to what it entails, namely that he is upon guidance. It is as if he said: "But I am upon guidance in the highest degree, because I am a messenger from Allah, glorified and exalted be He."

﴿Uballighukum risālāti rabbī wa-anṣaḥu lakum wa-aʿlamu mina llāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ (I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give you sincere counsel, and I know from Allah what you do not know) are attributes of "a messenger," or a new independent clause (istiʾnāf); on both readings their purpose is to explain that he is a messenger. Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿Uballighukum﴾ with the lightened form (takhfīf). He used the plural "messages" (risālāt) either because they differ in their times, or because their meanings are diverse, such as beliefs, admonitions and rulings; or because what is meant by them is what was revealed to him and to the prophets before him, such as the scrolls of Shith and Idris. The addition of the lām in ﴿lakum﴾ (to you) serves to indicate that his counsel was purely sincere toward them. As for ﴿aʿlamu mina llāhi﴾ (I know from Allah), it is a confirmation of what he threatened them with, for its meaning is: "I know of His power and the severity of His seizing," or: "I know from Him, through revelation, things of which you have no knowledge."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 63–64:

﴿Are you amazed⁠—﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle, here expressing denial/disapproval) and the waw (conjunction) for coordination with an elided element, meaning: "Did you deny and were you amazed?" ﴿that there has come to you﴾ meaning: that there has come to you ﴿a reminder from your Lord﴾, i.e., a message or an admonition. ﴿through a man﴾, i.e., through the tongue of a man ﴿from among you﴾, i.e., from among your own group or from your own kind, for they used to marvel at the sending of a human being and would say: (Had God willed, He would have sent down angels; we never heard of this among our forefathers of old). ﴿so that he may warn you﴾ of the consequence of disbelief and sins. ﴿and so that you may be wary﴾ of them because of the warning. ﴿and that you may receive mercy﴾ through piety. The purpose of the particle of hope (la'alla, "perhaps/so that") is to draw attention to the fact that piety is not a necessitating cause, and that receiving mercy from God, exalted is He, is an act of grace; and that the one who is pious should not rely on his piety nor feel safe from the punishment of God, exalted is He.

﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him﴾, and they were those who believed in him, and they were forty men and forty women. It is also said they were nine: his sons Sam, Ham and Japheth, and six of those who believed in him. ﴿in the ark﴾: this is related either to "with him" or to "We saved him," or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the relative pronoun or from the pronoun in "with him." ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ by the flood. ﴿Indeed, they were a blind people﴾, blind of heart, not discerning. Its original form was ʿamiyyin, which was lightened (to ʿamin), and it has been read as ʿaminan ("blind"); the former (ʿamiyyin) is more emphatic because it indicates persistence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 63–64:

﴿Are you amazed⁠—﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle, here expressing denial/disapproval) and the waw (conjunction) for coordination with an elided element, meaning: "Did you deny and were you amazed?" ﴿that there has come to you﴾ meaning: that there has come to you ﴿a reminder from your Lord﴾, i.e., a message or an admonition. ﴿through a man﴾, i.e., through the tongue of a man ﴿from among you﴾, i.e., from among your own group or from your own kind, for they used to marvel at the sending of a human being and would say: (Had God willed, He would have sent down angels; we never heard of this among our forefathers of old). ﴿so that he may warn you﴾ of the consequence of disbelief and sins. ﴿and so that you may be wary﴾ of them because of the warning. ﴿and that you may receive mercy﴾ through piety. The purpose of the particle of hope (la'alla, "perhaps/so that") is to draw attention to the fact that piety is not a necessitating cause, and that receiving mercy from God, exalted is He, is an act of grace; and that the one who is pious should not rely on his piety nor feel safe from the punishment of God, exalted is He.

﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him﴾, and they were those who believed in him, and they were forty men and forty women. It is also said they were nine: his sons Sam, Ham and Japheth, and six of those who believed in him. ﴿in the ark﴾: this is related either to "with him" or to "We saved him," or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the relative pronoun or from the pronoun in "with him." ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ by the flood. ﴿Indeed, they were a blind people﴾, blind of heart, not discerning. Its original form was ʿamiyyin, which was lightened (to ʿamin), and it has been read as ʿaminan ("blind"); the former (ʿamiyyin) is more emphatic because it indicates persistence.

﴿And to ʿĀd, their brother Hūd﴾: He is conjoined to "Nūḥ" (ﷺ) [in the sense of being sent] to his people. [Hūd] is an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) to "their brother." The intended meaning is one of them, as when they say "O brother of the Arabs" to one of them. He is Hūd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabāḥ ibn al-Khulūd ibn ʿĀd ibn ʿŪṣ ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ. It is also said that he is Hūd ibn Shālaḥ ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ, the paternal cousin of ʿĀd's father. He was described as one of them because they were the most able to understand his speech, the most aware of his circumstances, and the most inclined to follow him.

﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him."﴾ He begins with this statement without conjunction, as if it were the answer to a questioner who asks, "What did he say to them when he was sent?" Their reply is likewise [presented without conjunction].

﴿Will you not then fear [Allah's punishment]?﴾ It seems that his people were closer [in time] to the people of Nūḥ, peace be upon him, and therefore he said, "Will you not then fear?"

﴿The eminent ones among his people who disbelieved said﴾: because among their nobles there were those who believed in him, such as Marthad ibn Saʿd.

(p-19) ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾: firmly established in lightness of intellect and persisting in it, in that you have abandoned the religion of your people. ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 67–69:

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?﴾ Its explanation has already been given. The prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, answering the disbelievers' foolish words with what they answered, and turning away from confronting them, reflects complete sincere counsel, compassion, humbling of the self, and good manner in argument. So it should be for every counselor. In His saying: ﴿And I am a trustworthy adviser to you﴾ there is an indication that they knew him to possess both qualities. Abu 'Amr (Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala') recited ﴿ubalighukum﴾ (I convey to you) in both places in this surah, and in al-Ahqaf, with a light (mukhaffaf) pronunciation. ﴿And remember when He made you successors (khulafa', sing. khalifah, "successors" or "vicegerents") after the people of Noah﴾: that is, in their dwellings, or in the land, by making you kings. For Shaddad ibn 'Ad was among those who ruled the inhabited earth from the sands of 'Alij to the trees of 'Oman. He warned them of the punishment of God, then reminded them of His favor. ﴿And He increased you in stature (bastah) in creation﴾: in height and strength. ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾: a generalization after a specification. ﴿That perhaps you may prosper﴾: so that the mention of the blessings may lead you to gratitude for them, which leads to prosperity.

﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship?"﴾ They found it far-fetched that worship be restricted to Allah and that they turn away from what their fathers associated with Him, out of absorption in imitation and love for what they had been accustomed to. The meaning of "coming" in ﴿Have you come to us﴾ is either coming from a place where he had withdrawn from his people, or coming from the sky in mockery, or intended figuratively, as in their saying "he went to revile me." ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of punishment, which is implied by His words ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in it.

﴿He said: "There has already fallen upon you﴾ it has become due and binding upon you, or it has descended upon you, on the basis that what is expected is treated as what has occurred ﴿from your Lord an abomination [rijs]﴾ a punishment, from "irtijas," which is agitation. ﴿And wrath﴾ the will to take vengeance. ﴿Do you dispute with me over names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority?﴾ That is, over things you named as gods, though they have no meaning of divinity, because the one who deserves worship in essence is the one who brought everything into being. And if they did deserve it, that deserving would be by God's appointment, either through sending down a sign or by establishing a proof. He showed that the ultimate of their argument and their support is that idols are called gods without any evidence indicating the reality of what is named. Attributing the designation to those whose words are not regarded displays the extreme of their ignorance and their excessive stupidity. It has been used as evidence that the name is the named, and that languages are tawqifiyyah (divinely taught, not merely human convention), for if that were not so, the censure and nullification would not be directed at them as "names invented for which Allah sent down no authority." The weakness of both views is evident. ﴿Then wait﴾ for the descent of the punishment upon you, since the truth has become clear while you persist in obstinacy. ﴿Indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾.

﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾ in the religion, ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾ toward them. ﴿And We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, We uprooted them. ﴿And they were not believers﴾ is an allusion (ta'ridh) to those among them who had believed, and a reminder that what distinguishes those who were saved from those who perished (p-20) is faith.

It is narrated that they worshipped idols, so God sent Hud to them, but they denied him and grew more insolent. God withheld the rain from them for three years until they were afflicted with hardship. At that time, when calamity struck, both believers and polytheists among the people would turn toward the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram) and ask God for relief. So they dispatched a delegation to it, Qayl ibn ʿAnz and Marthad ibn Saʿd, along with seventy of their notables. At that time in Mecca were the Amalaqa, the sons of ʿAmlaq ibn Lawadh ibn Sam, and their chief was Muʿawiya ibn Bakr. When they came to him, while he was outside Mecca, he lodged them and honored them, for they were his maternal uncles and in-laws. They stayed with him for a month, drinking wine, while two singing-girls of his, al-Jaradatan, sang to them. When he saw them so absorbed in amusement that they had forgotten what they had been sent for, it troubled him, and he was ashamed to speak to them about it, fearing they would think he found their stay burdensome. So he taught the two singing-girls:

Ah, O Qayl, woe to you, arise and call out, perhaps God will give us the clouds to drink,
So that He may water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd
Have become such that they can no longer speak clearly.

They sang it to them until it disturbed them. Marthad said: "By God, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your Prophet and repent to God, Glorified and Exalted is He, you will be watered." They said to Muʿawiya: "Keep him away from us, let him not come with us to Mecca, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion." Then they entered Mecca, and Qayl said: "O God, water ʿAd as You used to water them." So God brought into being three clouds: a white one, a red one, and a black one. Then a caller called to him from the sky: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and for your people." He said: "I choose the black one, for it contains the most water." So it set out upon ʿAd from the valley of al-Mughith. They rejoiced at it and said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾. But a barren wind came out of it and destroyed them, while Hud and the believers with him were saved. They then came to Mecca and worshipped God, Glorified and Exalted is He, there until they died.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 73:

﴿And to Thamud﴾ (a tribe of the Arabs) ﴿their brother Salih﴾. They were called after their oldest forefather, Thamud ibn Athir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

It is also said that they were named after the scarcity of their water, from al-thamad (ثمد), which means little water. It is read as unvoiced (maṣrūfan, مَصْرُوفًا), either by interpreting it as the tribe (al-hayy, الحَيّ) or by considering the original form (al-aṣl, الأصْل). Their dwellings were al-Hijr (الحِجْر), between the Hijaz and al-Sham (Syria), extending to Wadi al-Qura. ﴿Their brother Salih﴾: Salih ibn Ubayd ibn Asaf ibn Masih ibn Ubayd ibn Hadhir ibn Thamud.

﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear proof (bayyinah) from your Lord﴾: a miracle whose evidence is manifest for the soundness of my prophethood.

His saying ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that proof. ﴿A sign (ayah, آيَةً)﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the governing element in it is the sense of pointing (al-ishara). ﴿For you﴾ specifies those for whom it is a sign. It is permissible for ﴿she-camel of Allah﴾ to be a substitute (badal) or an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan), with ﴿for you﴾ as the predicate governing ﴿ayah﴾. The attribution of the she-camel to Allah is for its glorification, and because it came from Him without intermediaries or familiar causes; for this reason it was a sign.

﴿So leave her to eat on Allah's earth﴾, that is, the herbage. ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾: He forbade the touching that is the prelude to harm, which encompasses all kinds of injury, as an intensification of the matter and a removal of excuse. ﴿Lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ is the response (jawab) to the prohibition.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 74–75:

﴿And remember when He made you successors after ʿAd and settled you in the land﴾, the land of al-Hijr. ﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾, meaning you build in its plains, or from the ease (suhūla) of the land, by what you make from it, such as bricks (labin) and kiln-fired bricks (ājurr). ﴿And you hew houses out of the mountains﴾. It is also read as "tanḥatūna" with a fatḥa, and as "tanḥātūna" with lengthened vowel (ishbāʿ). The accusative of "buyūtan" (houses) is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a state of the subject) that is anticipated (muqaddara), or an object (mafʿūl), on the understanding that the sense is "houses from the mountains." Or "tanḥitūna" carries the meaning of "tattakhidhūna" (you take). ﴿So remember the bounties of God and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief.﴾

﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said﴾, meaning arrogant towards faith. ﴿To those who were deemed weak﴾, meaning to those whom they deemed weak and humbled. ﴿To those among them who believed﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for "alladhīna ustuḍʿifū," a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull) if the pronoun refers to "his people," and a substitute of part (badal al-baʿḍ) if it refers to "alladhīna" (those who were deemed weak). Ibn ʿĀmir read "wa-qāla al-malaʾu" with a waw. ﴿Do you know that Ṣāliḥ is one sent from his Lord?﴾ They said this in mockery. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with."﴾ They turned away from the straightforward answer, which is "naʿam" (yes), drawing attention to the fact that his being sent is too evident for any sensible person to doubt or for people of judgment to be unaware of. The matter in question is only who believed in him and who disbelieved, and therefore he said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 76–77:

﴿The arrogant ones among his people said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you believed in."﴾ This is in the form of opposition (ʿalā wajh al-muqābalah), and they placed "you believed in it" (āmantum bihi) in the position of "it was sent with it" (ursila bihi), as a rejection of what they had made a known and accepted matter.

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾, that is, they slaughtered her. The action of some of them was attributed to all of them because of their association with it (li-l-mulābasah), or because it was done with their approval (li-annahu kāna bi-riḍāhum). ﴿And they defied the command of their Lord﴾, and were arrogant toward obeying it, which is what Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, had conveyed to them with his words: ﴿"Leave her alone"﴾. ﴿And they said: "O Ṣāliḥ, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are indeed among the messengers."﴾
