Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 78–79:

﴿So the quake seized them⦆ (al-Zalzala, the earthquake). ﴿And they became, in their abode, lifeless corpses fallen prone﴾ (khamidin, extinguished; mayyitin, dead).

It is narrated: After ʿAd, they (the Thamud) resettled their lands, succeeded them, and multiplied, and they were granted long lifespans, such that dwellings could not contain them. So they hewed houses out of the mountains. They lived in abundance and plenty, but they transgressed and spread corruption in the land and worshipped idols. So God sent to them Salih, one of their nobles, and he warned them. They asked him for a sign, and he said, "What sign do you want?" They said, "Go out with us to our festival, and you will call upon your God, and we will call upon our gods; whoever is answered, he shall be followed." So he went out with them, and they called upon their idols, but these did not answer them. Then their chief Jundaʿ ibn ʿAmr pointed to a solitary rock called al-Kathiba and said to him, "Bring forth from this rock a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and hairless (ʿushra, jawfa, wabra). If you do so, we will believe you." Salih took a covenant from them: "If I do this, you will surely believe." They said, "Yes." So he prayed and called upon his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour with her child, and it split open, bringing forth a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and hairless, just as they had described, while they looked on. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundaʿ believed, along with a group, but the rest were prevented from faith by Dhuʾab ibn ʿAmr, al-Habab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sughr, their soothsayer.

The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing the trees and coming to the water on alternate days. She would not lift her head from the well until she had drunk all that was in it, and then she would stretch her legs apart, and they would milk as much as they wished until their vessels were full; so they drank and stored. She used to summer on the upper part of the valley, whereupon their livestock would flee to its lower part, and she would winter in the lower part, whereupon their herds would flee to its upper part. This grieved them. ʿUnayza, the mother of Ghanim, and Sadaqa, the daughter of al-Mukhtar, adorned for them the slaughter of her, so they hamstrung her and divided her flesh. Her young one climbed a mountain called Qarra and cried out three times. Salih said to them, "Seize the young one, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you." But they could not overtake it, for the rock split open after its cry and it entered it. Then Salih said to them, "Tomorrow your faces will become yellow, and the day after, red, and on the third day, black. Then the punishment will overtake you in the morning." When they saw the signs, they sought to kill him, but God delivered him to the land of Palestine. When it was the forenoon of the fourth day, they perfumed themselves with aloe (al-Sabr) and wrapped themselves in leather shrouds (al-Anta‘). Then a cry came upon them from the sky, and their hearts were torn apart, and they perished.

(p-22) ﴿So he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who advise﴾. Its apparent meaning is that his turning away from them was after he had seen them lying prone. Perhaps he addressed them with it after their destruction, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed the people of the well of Badr and said: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?"

Or he mentioned that by way of lamenting over them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 78–79:

﴿So the quake seized them⦆ (al-Zalzala, the earthquake). ﴿And they became, in their abode, lifeless corpses fallen prone﴾ (khamidin, extinguished; mayyitin, dead).

It is narrated: After ʿAd, they (the Thamud) resettled their lands, succeeded them, and multiplied, and they were granted long lifespans, such that dwellings could not contain them. So they hewed houses out of the mountains. They lived in abundance and plenty, but they transgressed and spread corruption in the land and worshipped idols. So God sent to them Salih, one of their nobles, and he warned them. They asked him for a sign, and he said, "What sign do you want?" They said, "Go out with us to our festival, and you will call upon your God, and we will call upon our gods; whoever is answered, he shall be followed." So he went out with them, and they called upon their idols, but these did not answer them. Then their chief Jundaʿ ibn ʿAmr pointed to a solitary rock called al-Kathiba and said to him, "Bring forth from this rock a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and hairless (ʿushra, jawfa, wabra). If you do so, we will believe you." Salih took a covenant from them: "If I do this, you will surely believe." They said, "Yes." So he prayed and called upon his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour with her child, and it split open, bringing forth a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and hairless, just as they had described, while they looked on. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundaʿ believed, along with a group, but the rest were prevented from faith by Dhuʾab ibn ʿAmr, al-Habab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sughr, their soothsayer.

The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing the trees and coming to the water on alternate days. She would not lift her head from the well until she had drunk all that was in it, and then she would stretch her legs apart, and they would milk as much as they wished until their vessels were full; so they drank and stored. She used to summer on the upper part of the valley, whereupon their livestock would flee to its lower part, and she would winter in the lower part, whereupon their herds would flee to its upper part. This grieved them. ʿUnayza, the mother of Ghanim, and Sadaqa, the daughter of al-Mukhtar, adorned for them the slaughter of her, so they hamstrung her and divided her flesh. Her young one climbed a mountain called Qarra and cried out three times. Salih said to them, "Seize the young one, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you." But they could not overtake it, for the rock split open after its cry and it entered it. Then Salih said to them, "Tomorrow your faces will become yellow, and the day after, red, and on the third day, black. Then the punishment will overtake you in the morning." When they saw the signs, they sought to kill him, but God delivered him to the land of Palestine. When it was the forenoon of the fourth day, they perfumed themselves with aloe (al-Sabr) and wrapped themselves in leather shrouds (al-Anta‘). Then a cry came upon them from the sky, and their hearts were torn apart, and they perished.

(p-22) ﴿So he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who advise﴾. Its apparent meaning is that his turning away from them was after he had seen them lying prone. Perhaps he addressed them with it after their destruction, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed the people of the well of Badr and said: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?"

Or he mentioned that by way of lamenting over them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 80–81:

﴿And Lot⦆ — that is, We sent Lot. ﴿When he said to his people﴾ — at the time he said to them; or, "Mention Lot," and "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for him. ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾ — a rebuke and reproach for that deed which persists in ugliness. ﴿That which no one in the worlds has committed before you﴾ — no one at all had done it before you. The letter "bi" (in bihā) is for transitivity (ta'diya), and the first "min" (min aḥad) is to emphasize the negation and its comprehensiveness (istighrāq), while the second "min" (min al-'ālamīn) is for partitive meaning (tab'iḍ). The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) that confirms the denunciation, as if he first rebuked them for committing the abomination and then for inventing it, for that is worse.

﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire, instead of women﴾ — an explanation of His saying: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾, and it is more forceful in denunciation and rebuke. Nafi' and Hafs read "innakum" (indeed you) as a fresh informative statement. "Shahwatan" (with desire) is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). In restricting it with desire, there is a description of them as purely animalistic, and an alert that a rational person should be motivated to physical union by the desire for offspring and the preservation of the species, not by the mere satisfaction of need. ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ — a turning away from denial to a statement about their condition that led them to commit the like of these acts, namely the habit of excess in everything; or a turning away from denial of this deed to blame for all their faults; or a turning away from denial to an omitted premise, such as: "There is no excuse for you in this; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 82–84:

﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your city."﴾ That is, they did not produce anything that would serve as an answer to his speech; rather, they met his counsel with a command to expel him and those of the believers who were with him from their city, and with ridicule of them. They said: ﴿"Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ That is, from the abominations.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ That is, those who believed in him. ﴿except his wife﴾ An exception from "his family," for she was concealing disbelief. ﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾ Among those who stayed in their dwellings and were thus destroyed. The masculine form is used because the males predominate.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾ That is, a kind of rain that was extraordinary, and it is explained by His saying: ﴿And We rained upon them a rain of stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Then look at how was the end of the criminals.﴾ It is narrated that Lut, son of Haran, son of Terah, when he emigrated with his paternal uncle Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to Syria, settled in al-Urdunn, and God sent him to the people of Sodom to call them to God and to forbid them from the indecency they had invented. They did not desist from it, so God rained stones upon them and they perished.

It is also said that those of them who remained were swallowed up by the earth, and stones rained upon those of them who were travelling.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 85:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb.﴾ That is, We sent [him] to them. They were the descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il (p-23) ibn Yasjur ibn Madyan. He was called the orator of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them all, for the excellence of his argumentation with his people. ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord.﴾ He means the miracle that was granted to him, though the Qur'an does not specify what it was. As for what is related about Musa's staff fighting the dragon, the birth of the sheep that the ram gave him, which were promised to him from their offspring, and the staff of Adam falling into his hand in the seven instances, these came after this exchange. It is possible that they were a karamah (a divinely granted marvel) for Musa, peace be upon him, or a irhas (a preparatory sign) for his prophethood.

﴿So give full measure⦆ That is, the instrument of measuring, by elision, or by applying "measure" to the measuring vessel, as in "living" for "livelihood." This is supported by His saying ﴿and the balance﴾, as He said in Surat Hud: ﴿Give full measure and weight﴾. Alternatively, "measure" means the act of measuring, and "balance" means the weighing with the balance. It is also permissible that "balance" be a verbal noun, like "mi'ad" (appointment).

﴿And do not diminish people's things⦆ Do not cheat them of their rights. He said "their things" for generality, to draw attention to the fact that they used to cheat in the great and the small, the little and the much. It was also said that they were profiteers who would not leave anything without cheating in it.

﴿And do not spread corruption in the earth⦆ by disbelief and injustice.

﴿After its reformation⦆ after its affairs had been set right, or after its people had been set right by the prophets and their followers through the sacred laws; or they had made it right. The attribution to it is like the attribution in ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾. 

﴿That is better for you, if you are believers⦆ This refers to acting upon what He commanded them and forbade them from. The meaning of "better" is either increase in general, or in humanity, good repute, and gathering wealth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 86–87:

﴿And do not sit at every path, threatening and turning away from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, and seeking to make it crooked.﴾ [Note: the Arabic text of 7:86 begins here with ﴿وَلا تَقْعُدُوا بِكُلِّ صِراطٍ تُوعِدُونَ﴾]

Let me correct my own rendering above, since the instruction is to keep the translation faithful and to include only the translated text. The full passage follows.

﴿وَلا تَقْعُدُوا بِكُلِّ صِراطٍ تُوعِدُونَ﴾ ("And do not sit at every path, threatening") — "every path" (bi-kulli ṣirāṭ) means every way of the religion, such as the Shaytan (Satan). The path of truth, although it is one, branches out into knowledge (ma'ārif), limits (ḥudūd) and rulings (aḥkām). Whenever they saw anyone striving toward any of these, they would prevent him. It is said that they used to sit at the lookout points (al-marāṣid) and say to whoever wished to go to Shu'ayb: "He is a liar, so let him not seduce you away from your religion," and they would threaten whoever believed in him. It is also said that they used to cut off the road.

﴿وَتَصُدُّونَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("and turning away from the way of Allah") — meaning the path on which they sat. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, as an explanation for "every path," and to indicate the magnitude of what they were turning people away from and to disparage what they were upon, or [it refers to] faith in Allah. ﴿مَن آمَنَ بِهِ﴾ ("those who believe in Him") — i.e., in Allah, or in every path according to the first view. "Man" (مَن) is the object of taṣuddūna (تَصُدُّونَ), by the principle of giving precedence to the nearer verb (i'māl al-aqrab). Had it been the object of tu'iddūna (تُوعِدُونَ), it would have said wa-taṣuddūnahum, and tu'iddūna would have been connected to what precedes it in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in taqʿudū (تَقْعُدُوا).

﴿وَتَبْغُونَها عِوَجًا﴾ ("and seeking to make it crooked") — and you seek for the way of Allah to be crooked, by casting doubts, or by describing it to the people as crooked.

﴿واذْكُرُوا إذْ كُنْتُمْ قَلِيلا﴾ ("And remember when you were few") — [in number] ʿadadakum (عَدَدَكم) or ʿuddatakum (عُدَدَكم) [in provisions].

﴿فَكَثَّرَكُمْ﴾ ("and He multiplied you") — through blessing in offspring or wealth.

﴿وانْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ المُفْسِدِينَ﴾ ("And look at how was the end of the corrupters") — of the nations before you; so take warning from them.

﴿وَإنْ كانَ طائِفَةٌ مِنكم آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي أُرْسِلْتُ بِهِ وطائِفَةٌ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا فاصْبِرُوا﴾ ("And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent, and a group who have not believed, then be patient") — i.e., wait (fa-tarabbaṣū).

﴿حَتّى يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ بَيْنَنا﴾ ("until Allah judges between us") — i.e., between the two groups, by granting victory to the righteous over the falsifiers. So it is a promise to the believers and a threat to the disbelievers.

﴿وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الحاكِمِينَ﴾ ("And He is the best of judges") — since there is no one to reverse His judgment and no injustice in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 88–89:

﴿The chiefs of those of his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you, from our town; or you will return to our religion."﴾ (p-24) That is, one of the two matters will certainly happen: either your expulsion from the town or your return to disbelief. Shu'ayb, upon him be peace, had never been in their religion at all, because prophets cannot be subject to disbelief in any way. But they treated the group as dominant over the one, so he and his people were addressed with their mode of address, and on this basis he framed the reply in his words: ﴿He said: "Even though we were unwilling?"﴾ That is, how could we return to it while we detest it, or would you make us return while we are in a state of aversion?

﴿We would have fabricated a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah had rescued us from it.﴾ The conditional clause has an omitted answer, whose indication is ﴿We would have fabricated a lie against Allah﴾. It is in the sense of the future, since it has not occurred, but it is treated as though it has occurred for emphasis. The particle "qad" (indeed, already) is placed before it to bring it close to the present: that is, "we have already fabricated a lie if we were to resolve to return after deliverance from it," inasmuch as we would then be claiming that Allah, exalted is He, has a rival, and that what we were upon is falsehood and what you are upon is truth. It has also been said that this is the response to an oath, its implied sense being: "By Allah, we would indeed have fabricated a lie."

﴿And it is not for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills.﴾ That is, abandonment by Him and our apostasy. In this there is evidence that disbelief occurs by the will of Allah. It has also been said that he intended by this to cut off their hope of his return, by making it conditional upon something that will not happen.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾ That is, His knowledge encompasses everything, what has been and what will be, from us and from you.

﴿In Allah we have put our trust.﴾ That He may keep us firm in faith and deliver us from the wicked.

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth.﴾ Judge between us and them. The "fattah" is the judge, and "fattahah" is judgment. Or: make our affair manifest, until what lies between us and them is uncovered and the true is distinguished from the false, from "fath" (opening) of a difficulty when one clarifies it.

﴿And You are the best of those who decide.﴾ According to both meanings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 90–91:

﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then indeed you will be losers."﴾ And abandon your religion. ﴿Indeed, you would then be losers﴾ because you would be exchanging his misguidance for your guidance, or because of the loss of what you would gain through defrauding and cheating in measure and weight. This serves in place of the response to the conditional clause and the oath preceded by the lam of emphasis.

﴿So the quake seized them﴾ the earthquake. And in surah al-Hijr: ﴿So the shout seized them﴾, and it may have been from its beginnings.

﴿So they became in their home, prostrate [lifeless]﴾ i.e., in their city.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 92–93:

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾ — that is, they were utterly uprooted, as if they had never lived there. Al-maghna means the dwelling place. ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers﴾ — in religion and in worldly life — not those who affirmed him and followed him, as they claimed; for they are the winners in both abodes. To draw attention to this and to emphasize it, he repeated the relative pronoun, began the two clauses afresh, and presented them both as nominal sentences.

﴿So he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and given you sincere counsel."﴾ He said this out of grief over them, because of the intensity of his sorrow for them. Then he disapproved of himself and said: ﴿"So how can I grieve over a people who are disbelievers?"﴾ They were not people deserving of grief, because of what befell them as a consequence of their disbelief. Or he said it as an excuse for not being more deeply grieved over them. The meaning is: I have indeed exerted myself in conveying and warning, and expended my utmost effort in counsel and compassion, but you did not believe my words, so how can I grieve over you? It is also read as ﴿fa-kayfa aysī﴾ with two imalahs (vocalic inclinations).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 94–95:

(p-25) ﴿And We never sent a prophet to a town without visiting its people with adversity and hardship﴾, that is, with misery and harm. ﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾, until they would beseech and abase themselves.

﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾, i.e., We gave them, in place of the affliction and hardship they had been in, safety and ease, as a trial for them with both conditions. ﴿Until they multiplied﴾, meaning they increased in number and in means. It is said: "ʿafā al-nabāt" (the plant grew abundantly) when it proliferates, and from this comes "iʿfāʾ al-liḥā" (letting the beard grow). ﴿And they said: "Adversity and prosperity have touched our forefathers"﴾, in ingratitude for God's blessing and forgetfulness of His remembrance, and in the belief that it is a custom of time that people are repaid with alternating adversity and prosperity, and that our forefathers had been touched by the same as what has touched us. ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾, unexpectedly. ﴿While they did not perceive﴾ the descent of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 96–97:

﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God﴾ — meaning the towns implied by His saying: ﴿And We sent not into any town a warner⁠—﴾ (7:94). It is said that it means Makkah and what surrounds it. ﴿Had believed and been mindful of God⁠—﴾ in place of their disbelief and disobedience. ﴿We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth⁠﴾ — We would have widened good things for them and made them easy for them from every direction. It is also said that what is meant is rain and vegetation. Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿lafataḥnā⁠﴾ with the doubling (of the ta, i.e. lafattaḥnā, for intensity). ﴿But they denied⁠﴾ the Messengers ﴿so We seized them for what they used to earn⁠﴾ of disbelief and sins.

﴿Do the people of the towns then feel secure⁠—﴾ this is conjoined to His saying: ﴿So We seized them suddenly while they were not aware⁠﴾ (7:95), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. The meaning: after all that, do the people of the towns feel secure ﴿that Our punishment will not come upon them by night⁠﴾ — as a tabyīt (act of coming by night), or at a time of bayāt (night), or as one who is made to spend the night, or as those made to spend the night. It is originally a verbal noun meaning al-baytūtah (the act of spending the night), and it comes with the meaning of al-tabyīt, like al-salām meaning al-taslīm (greeting). ﴿While they are sleeping⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to their pronoun, either the explicit one or the implicit one, in bayātan.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 98–99:

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or") with a sukun (a silent vowel), indicating repetition (al-tardid, alternation between the two questions). ﴿That Our punishment will come upon them in the forenoon﴾ (duha), meaning the late morning, when the sun has risen high; in origin it is the light of the sun once it has risen. ﴿While they are playing﴾, meaning amusing themselves out of extreme heedlessness, or occupying themselves with what does not benefit them.

﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ This is a repetition of His saying ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure?﴾ The "plan of Allah" (makr Allah) is a metaphor for gradually leading the servant on (istidraj) and seizing him from where he does not expect. ﴿None feel secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are lost﴾, those who have lost by disbelief and by neglecting reflection and consideration.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 100:

﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth after its previous people?﴾ That is, they succeed those who passed before them and inherit their dwellings. The verb yahdi (to make clear, to guide) is construed here with the preposition lam (li) because it carries the meaning of yubayyinu (to make evident). ﴿That if We willed, We would smite them for their sins⦆ — that is, the matter being that if We willed, We would smite them for the recompense of their sins, as We smote those before them. Here "that" (an) is the subject (fa'il) of yahdi. Whoever reads it with the nun (naun, "We") makes it an object (maf'ul). ﴿And We seal upon their hearts⦆ — this is conjoined to what is indicated by the sense (ma dalla 'alayhi), or to the verb "has it not become clear" in the sense that they are heedless of guidance; or it is a separate sentence, in the sense of "and We seal," and it is not permissible to conjoin it to "We would smite them," taking it to mean "and We had sealed," because it is within the context of the conditional, and the answer of "law" (lau) is the verb, since it would lead to negating the sealing from them. ﴿So they do not hear⦆ — hearing that comprehends and takes heed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 101–102:

﴿Those are the cities﴾, meaning the cities of the nations just mentioned. ﴿We relate to you some of their news﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) if "the cities" is taken as the predicate (khabar), and its meaning is then restricted by the word "some" (bi-l-taqyīd bihā). It is a predicate (khabar) if "the cities" is taken as a qualifier (ṣifah). It is also permissible for the two to be two predicates. The word ﴿min﴾ is partitive (min li-l-tab'īḍ), meaning: We relate some of their news, and they have other news that We do not relate. ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning with miracles. ﴿So they were not going to believe﴾ when they came with them. ﴿In what they had denied before﴾, meaning in what they had denied before the messengers. Rather, they remained persistent in denial. Or it means: they were not going to believe during the whole span of their lives in what they had denied at first, when the messengers came to them, and their long-lasting call and the successive signs did not affect them at all. The lām in ﴿liyu'minū﴾ is for emphasizing the negation and indicates that they were not fit for belief, because belief is incompatible with their state of determination in unbelief and the sealing of their hearts. ﴿Thus does God seal the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, so their resolve does not soften through the signs and the warnings. ﴿And We did not find in most of them﴾, meaning in most people. The verse is a parenthetical statement, or it refers to most of the nations mentioned. ﴿Any covenant﴾, meaning any fulfilment of a covenant, for most of them broke what God had covenanted with them concerning faith and piety, through the sending down of signs and the establishment of proofs. Or it means what they had pledged when they were in harm and fear, like ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾. ﴿And indeed We found most of them﴾, meaning We knew them.

﴿to be deviators﴾. It is derived from "I found Zayd," with the verb's first object... Specifically, the construction is governed by the lightened inna (mukhaffafah, the lightened form of inna) and the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqah), and this is not permitted except with the subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar) and the verbs that enter upon them. According to the Kufan grammarians, inna here serves for negation, and the lām carries the meaning of "illā" (except).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 103–105:

﴿Then We sent after them Moses﴾. The pronoun refers either to the messengers mentioned in His words ﴿And there had certainly come to them their messengers﴾, or to the nations. ﴿With Our signs﴾, meaning the miracles. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged them﴾, by disbelieving in them instead of believing in them, which is what they deserved because of their clarity. For this reason, ﴿wronged﴾ was used in place of ﴿disbelieved﴾. ''Pharaoh'' is a title for whoever ruled Egypt, like Khosrow (Kisra) for whoever ruled Persia; his name was Qabus, and it was said to be al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan. ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾.

﴿And Moses said, "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds"﴾ to you. His words ﴿It is fitting for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth﴾ are perhaps a response to Pharaoh's denial of him regarding his claim to prophethood. It was not mentioned because the words ﴿but they wronged them﴾ indicate it. The original form was (ḥaqīqun ʿalayya an lā aqūla), as Nafi' recited, and it was inverted to avoid confusion, like the line: "And the spears are wretched with the donkey-like fools." Or because what is obligatory for you is also obligatory on the one to whom it applies. Or for emphasis in describing him with truthfulness. The meaning is that it is a binding obligation upon the one who speaks the truth that I should be the one who speaks it; He is not pleased except with one like me speaking it. Or ḥaqīq is taken to imply ḥarīṣ (eager). Or ʿalā is put in place of bāʾ to indicate firm attachment, as in their saying: "I shot upon the bow" and "I came upon a good state." Abiy's recitation with bāʾ supports this. It was also read as ḥaqīqun an lā aqūla without ʿalā. ﴿Indeed I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel﴾, that you release them so that they may return with me to the holy land, which is the homeland of their fathers. He had enslaved them and made them serve in labors.(p-27)

﴿He said, "If you have brought a sign, then produce it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is, from the One who sent you. ﴿Then produce it﴾: bring it before me, so that your truthfulness may be established by it. ﴿If you are of the truthful﴾: in your claim.

﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾: its matter was manifest, and there was no doubt that it was a serpent, that is, a great snake.

It is related that when he threw it, it became a serpent, a male serpent (ash'ar), with its mouth wide open, between its jaws eighty cubits. It placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned towards Pharaoh, and he fled from it and defecated. The people fled in a crowd, and twenty-five thousand of them died. Pharaoh cried out, "O Musa, I implore you by He who sent you, take it, and I will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." So he took it, and it returned to being a staff.

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ from his pocket, or from under his armpit. ﴿And behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾: that is, white with a whiteness outside the ordinary, which the spectators gathered to observe; or white to the observers, not that it was white by its natural constitution.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, was intensely dark-complexioned, so he put his hand into his pocket, or under his armpit, then drew it out, and behold, it was white, luminous, its radiance overpowering the radiance of the sun.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 109–112:

﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer, knowing."﴾ It is said that he (i.e., Pharaoh) and the nobles of his people said this by way of consultation regarding his matter. It is related of him in Surat ash-Shu'ara' (the Poets), and of them here.

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾ You point out what we should do.

﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers,﴾

﴿who will bring you every skilled sorcerer."﴾ It is as if their opinions agreed upon this, so they pointed it out to Pharaoh. Al-irja' (putting off) means delay, i.e., delay his matter. Its original form is urji'uhu, as Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read, from arja'tu (urji'uhu). Likewise, "arji'hu" (with a hamza and the pronoun) according to the reading of Ibn Kathir, following the original form of the pronoun; or "arjihi" from arjaytu, as Nafi' read in the narration of Warsh, and Isma'il and al-Kisa'i. As for his reading in the narration of Qalun, ﴿arjih﴾ with the omission of the yā', it is for the sufficiency of the kasra in place of it. As for the reading of Hamzah, 'Asim and Hafs, "arjih" with a sukun on the ha', it is by analogy of the separated (pronoun) to the connected, and ﴿arjih﴾ is treated like ibl (camels) in the sukun of its middle. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, "arji'hi" with a hamza and a kasra on the ha', the grammarians do not approve of it, for the ha' is not given a kasra except when preceded by a kasra or a silent yā'; its rationale is that the hamza, when it was changed to a yā', was given its treatment. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-kulli sahharin" (every cunning sorcerer) in this place and in Surah Yunus, and their agreement upon it in ash-Shu'ara' supports it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 113–114:

﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾ after he had sent the police (al-shurtah) in pursuit of them. ﴿They said: Indeed for us there will surely be a reward, if we are the victors﴾. This is resumed (isti'naf) as if it were the answer to a questioner who asks: "What did they say when they came?" Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Hafs, on the authority of Asim, recited ﴿inna lana la-ajran﴾ as a declarative statement affirming the reward, as if they were saying: "A reward is indispensable for us." The indefinite form (al-tankir) here indicates magnification (li'l-ta'zim).

﴿He said: Yes﴾, indeed for you there will be a reward. ﴿And indeed you will be among those brought near﴾. This is conjoined (ʿutifa) to what takes the place of ﴿yes﴾, with an addition beyond the answer in order to encourage them (li-tahridihim).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 115–116:

﴿They said: "O Musa, either you throw, or we become the throwers."﴾ They gave Musa the choice out of regard for good manners (adab), or to display confidence (al-jaladah). Yet their desire was to throw first, so they hinted at it by altering the structure of the speech to something more emphatic: defining the predicate (ta'rif al-khabar), placing the separating pronoun in the middle (tawsit al-fasl), or emphasizing their attached pronoun with a detached one (ta'kid damirihim al-muttasil bi-al-munfasil). Therefore He said: ﴿"Nay, you throw!"﴾ out of generosity and leniency, or out of contempt for them and confidence in his own standing. ﴿So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ by making them imagine what the reality was not. ﴿And they struck them with terror﴾ and frightened them with intense fright, as if they had sought to be feared. ﴿And they produced a great magic﴾ in its craft.

It is narrated that they threw thick ropes and long sticks, as if they were serpents filling the valley, and some of them mounted upon others.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 117–119:

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff."﴾ So he threw it down, and it became a serpent. ﴿And behold, it swallowed up what they had fabricated﴾, i.e., what they were falsifying of deception (ifk), and ifk is diversion and turning a thing away from its face. It is permissible that ma be a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), and it, together with the verb, carries the meaning of a passive object (maf'ul), i.e., "what was fabricated."

It is narrated that when it swallowed up their ropes and staffs and devoured them entirely, it turned toward the spectators, so they fled and crowded together until a great multitude perished. Then Moses took it, and it became a staff as it had been. The sorcerers said: "If this were sorcery, our ropes and our staffs would have remained."

Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿تَلْقَفُ﴾ (talqafu) here and in Ta-Ha and ash-Shu'ara'.

﴿So the truth was established﴾, i.e., it was confirmed because its matter became manifest. ﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾ of sorcery and counter-magic.

﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humiliated﴾, i.e., they became abased and bewildered; or they returned to the city humbled and subdued. The pronoun refers to Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 120–122:

﴿And the magicians were made to fall down prostrate.﴾ He made them fall upon their faces, as an indication that the truth overwhelmed them and compelled them to prostrate, to the point that they had no self-control left. Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verses 123–124:

﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in Him"﴾, meaning in God, or in Moses? The interrogative here (*al-istifham*, interrogation) is for denunciation (*al-inkar*). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr (from 'Asim), Ruh (from Ya'qub) and Hisham read with the two hamzahs fully articulated (*tahqiq al-hamzatayn*), according to the original form. Hafs read ﴿āmantum bihi﴾ as a declarative statement (*ʿalā al-ikhbār*). Qunbul read ﴿qāla Fir'awnu﴾, and for ﴿āmantum﴾ he replaces, in continuous recitation (*ḥāl al-waṣl*), the interrogative hamzah with an open waw (*wāwan maftūḥatan*), and lengthens after it by an elongation estimated at two alifs. In Ta-Ha he read it as a statement with a hamzah and an alif, and in al-Shu'ara' as an interrogative with a hamzah and an extended elongation estimated at two alifs. The rest read with the first hamzah fully articulated and the second softened (*talyin al-thāniyah*). ﴿Before I give you permission. Indeed this is a plot that you have plotted﴾, meaning: indeed this deed is a stratagem that you and Moses have devised. ﴿In the city﴾, meaning in Egypt, ﴿before you go out to the appointed meeting﴾. ﴿So that you may expel from it its people﴾, meaning the Copts, ﴿and the land may be cleared for you and for the Children of Israel﴾. ﴿But you will come to know﴾ the outcome of what you have done. This is a general threat (*tahdīd mujmal*), whose detail is: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides﴾, meaning from each side a limb. ﴿Then I will surely crucify you all﴾, as public disgrace for you and as an exemplary punishment for those like you. It is said that he was the first to establish this practice, and God legislated it for highwaymen as a way of magnifying their crime; for this reason He named it "warring against God and His Messenger." However, it is applied in sequence (*ʿalā al-taʿāqub*), out of the abundance of His mercy.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 125–126:**

﴿They said: Indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾ By death, without doubt; so we do not care about your threat. Or: indeed we are returning to our Lord and His reward, if you do that to us. It is as if they found it sweet, out of their intense longing (*shaghaf*) for meeting Allah. Or: our destiny and your destiny is to our Lord, and He will judge between us.

﴿And you resent nothing in us﴾ — that is, you disapprove of nothing in us. ﴿except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us.﴾ This is the best of deeds and the root of virtues. It is not something from which we could turn away in order to seek your approval. Then they turned for refuge to Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience.﴾ Pour upon us patience that overwhelms us, as water is poured out; or pour upon us that which purifies us from sins, and that is patience in the face of Pharaoh's threat. ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾ — steadfast in Islam. It was said that he did to them what he had threatened them with. It was also said that he was not able to overcome them, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You two and whoever follows you will be the victors.﴾

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 127:**

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?"﴾ By turning the people against you and calling them to oppose you. ﴿And [will they leave] you﴾ *wa-yadharaka* is conjoined (*'atf*) to *yufsidu* ("cause corruption"). Alternatively, it is the answer (*jawab*) to the interrogative, with the *wa* (and) functioning as in the verse of al-Hutay'a:

Was I not your neighbour, and between me and you were affection and brotherhood?

The meaning is: "Will it be that you leave Moses, and that he leaves you?" It has also been read with *raf'* (the nominative), on the basis that it is conjoined to *andhara* (he warns), or that it is a new clause (*isti'naf*), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It has also been read with *sukun* (the jussive), as if it were said: "*yufsidu wa-yadharaka*" (they cause corruption and leave you), like the words of God Most High: ﴿So I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾. ﴿And your gods﴾ meaning your objects of worship. It is said that he used to worship the stars. It is also said that he made idols for his people and ordered them to worship them, seeking closeness to him, and for this reason he said: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾. It has also been read *ilahatak*, meaning your worship.

﴿He said﴾: Pharaoh said, ﴿"We will kill their sons and spare their women"﴾, as we used to do before, so that it would be known that we are still in the same position of domination and dominance, and so that no one would imagine that he is the boy about whom the astrologers and soothsayers ruled that our kingdom would perish at his hands. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read *sanaqtulu* with the lightened form (*takhfif*). ﴿And indeed we are above them, dominant﴾: victorious, while they are subdued under our hands.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 128–129:

﴿Moses said to his people, "Seek help in Allah and be patient."﴾ When they heard the words of Pharaoh and grew restless because of them, he said this to calm them. ﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants.﴾ This is a consolation for them and an affirmation of the command to seek help in Allah and to remain steadfast in the matter. ﴿And the final outcome is for the God-conscious.﴾ (p-30) It is a promise to them of victory and a reminder of what He had promised them: the destruction of the Copts and the inheritance of their homes for them, and a confirmation of it. It has also been read as "wal-'aqibata" (with a fatha), in coordination with the subject of inna (the noun after inna, i.e., "al-ard"). The lam in "al-ard" may indicate either a specific reference (al-'ahd) or the genus (al-jins).

﴿They said﴾, that is, the Children of Israel: ﴿"We were harmed before you came to us"﴾ with the message, through the killing of the sons, ﴿"and after you came to us"﴾ with its renewal.

﴿He said, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land"﴾, a clear statement of what he had alluded to at first, when he saw that they were not consoled by that. He used the verb of hope ('asa) probably because he was not certain that they themselves, in their persons, would be the ones made successors, or their children. ﴿"And He will see how you act."﴾ That is, He will see what you do of gratitude and ingratitude, obedience and disobedience, and then He will recompense you according to what is found in you.

It has been narrated that Egypt was only opened for them in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 130–131:

﴿And We certainly afflicted the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾ — with droughts, due to the scarcity of rain and water. The word "sanah" (year) came to dominate over the sense of a year of famine, because of how much it is mentioned and used to date events, and from it was then derived the expression "asinat al-qawm," meaning the people were struck by drought. ﴿And a loss of fruits﴾ — through the abundance of blights.

﴿So that they might take heed﴾ — so that they would become aware that this was due to the ill omen of their disbelief and their disobedience, and thus be admonished; or that their hearts would be softened by hardships, so that they would turn in supplication to God and desire what is with Him.

﴿But when good came to them﴾ — of fertility and plenty. ﴿They said, "This is ours"﴾ — it is for us, and we deserve it. ﴿But if evil afflicted them﴾ — barrenness and calamity. ﴿They ascribed it to omen of Moses and those with him﴾ — they regarded them as a bad omen and said: "This has befallen us only because of them." This is an exaggeration in describing them as dull-witted and hard-hearted, for hardships soften hearts, humble stubborn dispositions and remove steadfastness, especially after witnessing the signs; yet these did not affect them, but rather increased their insolence and their immersion in error. He defined and mentioned "the good" (al-hasanah) with the particle of confirmation because it occurs frequently and the will is directly tied to bringing it about, and he made "the evil" (al-sayyi'ah) indefinite and introduced it with the particle of doubt because it is rare and is not intended for its own sake, but only incidentally. ﴿Indeed, their omen is with God﴾ — that is, the cause of their good and their evil is with Him, namely His judgment and His will; or the cause of their ill omen is with God, namely their deeds recorded with Him, for it is these that brought upon them what displeased them. It is also read "innama tayruhum," which is a collective noun; and it has been said that it is a plural. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ — that what befalls them is from God Most High, or from the ill omen of their deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 132–133:

﴿And they said, "Whatever (mahma)"﴾ Its origin is ma, the conditional particle, to which the superfluous ma has been added for emphasis; then its alif was changed into a hamza-less hā' (ha') because of the difficulty of the repetition.

It is also said that it is a compound of mah, the word uttered with the kaf (i.e., the sound used to call or to silence a beast), and ma, the response particle (ma al-jaza'iyyah). Its position in the sentence is nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), or accusative, by a verb that it explains.

﴿"Whatever sign you bring us, to enchant us with it"﴾ That is: whatever kind of thing comes before us, bring us with it. ﴿"a sign"﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of mahma. They called it a sign only according to Musa's claim, not because of their own belief; for this reason they said: ﴿"that you may enchant us with it, but we will not believe you"﴾, that is, to enchant our eyes with it and confuse us. The pronoun in "bihi" and "biha" refers to mahma: he mentioned it first according to its wording, and then made it feminine afterwards according to its meaning.

﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾: water that overflowed them and covered their dwellings and their fields, from rain or a torrent. It is also said it was smallpox, and it is also said it was plague, and it is also said it was pestilence. ﴿"and the locusts and the lice"﴾: it is said the lice are large ticks, and it is said they are the young of locusts before their wings grow.

﴿"and the frogs and the blood"﴾: It is narrated that they were rained upon for eight days in intense darkness, so that no one could leave his house, and water entered their houses until they stood in it up to their collarbones, while the houses of the Children of Israel were interlaced with theirs, so not a drop entered them; and it stood over their lands, preventing them from tilling and from using them. This lasted for them a week, and they said to Musa: ﴿"Pray to your Lord for us"﴾ that He may remove it from us, and we will believe in you. He prayed, and it was lifted from them, and there grew for them vegetation and crops the like of which had not been known; but they did not believe. Then Allah sent upon them the locusts, which ate their crops and fruits, then began to eat the doors, the ceilings, and the clothes; so they fled to him a second time, and he prayed and went out to the desert and pointed with his staff toward the east and the west, and they returned to the regions from which they had come; but they did not believe. Then Allah let loose upon them the lice, which consumed what the locusts had left; it would fall into their food and enter between their garments and their skins and suck them; so they fled to him, and he lifted it from them. They said: "Now we are certain that you are a sorcerer." Then Allah sent upon them the frogs, so that no cloth or food was uncovered without frogs being found in it; their beds were filled with them, they would leap into their cooking pots while they were boiling, and into their mouths when they spoke. They fled to him and humbled themselves, so he took covenants from them and prayed, and Allah lifted it from them; then they broke the covenants. Then Allah sent upon them blood, so their waters became blood, until a Copt and an Israelite would gather at one vessel, and what was on the Copt's side would be blood while what was on the Israelite's side would be water; and the water would be sucked from the Israelite's mouth and become blood in his mouth.

It is also said that Allah sent upon them nosebleeds. ﴿"signs"﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). ﴿"clearly detailed"﴾: made clear, such that no intelligent person would be confused that they are the signs of Allah and His punishment upon them; or detailed, for testing their conditions, since between every two of them there was a month, and the duration of each one was a week. It is also said that Musa remained among them after the sorcerers were defeated for twenty years, showing them these signs at leisure. ﴿"But they were arrogant"﴾ toward faith. ﴿"and they were a criminal people"﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 134–135:

﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) befell them﴾: meaning the detailed punishment, or the plague (al-ta'un) which Allah sent upon them after that. ﴿They said: "O Musa, pray to your Lord for us, by what He has covenanted with you"﴾: by His covenant with you, which is prophethood; or by that which He covenanted to you, that you should call upon Him with it, and He would answer you as He answered you in your signs. This is either a complement (silah) of "pray" (ud'u), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in it, meaning "pray to Allah seeking nearness to Him through what He has covenanted with you." Or it is connected to a deleted verb indicated by their entreaty, such as "grant us help in what we ask of you, by the right of what has been covenanted with you." Or it is an oath whose answer is His saying: ﴿"If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you and surely send the Children of Israel with you"﴾; that is, "We swear by the covenant of Allah with you that if you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe and surely send them."

﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, for a term which they were to reach﴾: up to a limit of time which they were to reach, whereupon they would be punished or destroyed in it. This is the time of drowning or death. It has been said: "up to a term they had set for their belief." ﴿Behold, they broke their word﴾: the answer of "when" (lamma), meaning: when We removed it from them, they immediately broke their word without deliberation or hesitation.

[7:136] So We took retribution from them: We intended to take vengeance upon them. Then We drowned them in the sea (al-yamm), that is, the sea whose depth cannot be reached. It was also said: its deep waters (lujjah).

[7:136] Because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them: that is, their drowning was due to their denial of the signs and their failure to reflect upon them, until they became like those heedless of them. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the retribution (al-niqmah), indicated by His saying: "So We took retribution."

[7:137] And We caused to inherit the people who had been oppressed (yustad'afun) through enslavement and the slaughter of their sons by their oppressors: the eastern and western parts of the earth (mashariq al-ard wa magharibaha). By this is meant the land of al-Sham, which the Children of Israel possessed after Pharaoh's people and the Amalekites, and established themselves in its regions. In which We had blessed: with fertility and abundance of livelihood. And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel: it took effect for them and was realised, the promise being fulfilled in its entirety, with support and establishment. This is His saying, may He be exalted: "And We wished to bestow favour" up to His saying: "that which they had feared." It was also read "kalimatu rabbika" (in the singular), because of the multiplicity of promises, owing to their patience (ma sabaru), that is, because of their steadfastness in hardships. And We destroyed (wa dammarna): and We ruined and demolished what Pharaoh and his people had built (ma kana yasna'u Fir'awnu wa qawmuhu) of palaces and edifices, and what they had been raising (wa ma kanu ya'rishun) of gardens or of buildings they erected, such as the palace (sarh) of Haman. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "ya'rishun" here and in al-Nahl with a dhammah (ya'rushun). This is the end of the story of Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 138:

And His saying: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾ and what follows is a mention of the shameful matters that the Children of Israel introduced after God had bestowed upon them great blessings and showed them great signs, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he saw from them, and as an awakening for the believers, so that they would not neglect calling themselves to account and watching over their own states.

It is narrated that Musa (peace be upon him) passed with them on the day of ʿAshura after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, and they fasted it in thanks.

﴿They came upon a people﴾ they passed by them. ﴿who were devoted to some idols they had﴾ who persisted in worshipping them. It is said they were images of cows, and that was the beginning of the affair of the calf. The people were of the ʿAmaliqa, whom Musa had been commanded to fight. And it is said they were from Lakhm. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yaʿkufūna﴾ with a kasra. ﴿They said: "O Musa, make for us a god"﴾ a likeness that we may worship. ﴿Just as they have gods﴾ which they worship, and "mā" is a particle that makes the "kāf" (as) govern a clause. ﴿He said: "Surely you are a people who act in ignorance"﴾ He described them with absolute ignorance and emphasized it, because what came from them after seeing the great signs was so far removed from reason.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 139–140:

﴿Indeed, these﴾ is a reference to the people. ﴿Will be destroyed﴾ means broken and ruined. ﴿What they are engaged in﴾ means that Allah demolishes their religion which they follow, smashes their idols and reduces them to fragments. ﴿And null﴾ means nullified and perished. ﴿What they used to do﴾ refers to their worship of them, even though they intended thereby to draw near to Allah, the Exalted. Indeed, he exaggerated in this statement by placing "these" as the subject of inna (indeed), by informing that what they are engaged in is destined for ruin (tabbar), and what they did is destined for nullification (butlan), and by placing the two predicates in the two sentences as predicates (khabar) of inna. This is to alert that destruction is inevitably overtaking what they are engaged in, and that total annihilation is necessarily attached to what they did, as a means of repulsion and warning against what they sought.

﴿He said: Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah﴾ meaning, shall I seek for you an object of worship? ﴿And He has favoured you over the worlds﴾ while the situation is that He has specially favoured you with blessings He did not give to others. In this there is an alert to the wrongness of their conduct, in that they responded to Allah's singling them out over their peers for what they did not deserve, by means of grace, by intending to associate with Him the lowliest of His creatures.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 141–142:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾: mention his favour toward you at this time. Ibn ʿĀmir recited "anjākum" (He delivered you).

﴿who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) explaining what they were delivered from. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the addressees, or to the people of Pharaoh, or to both.

(p-33) ﴿who slaughtered your sons and spared your women﴾: this is an explanatory substitute (badal mubayyin) for what precedes. ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾: in the deliverance or the torment there was a great blessing or a great ordeal.

﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights﴾: these were the nights of Dhu al-Qaʿdah. Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub recited "wawaʿadnā" (We promised). ﴿And We completed them with ten﴾: from Dhu al-Ḥijjah. ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was complete at forty nights﴾: reaching forty.

It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, had promised the Children of Israel in Egypt that after the destruction of Pharaoh he would bring them a Book from God containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should avoid. When Pharaoh was destroyed, he asked his Lord, and God commanded him to fast thirty days. When he had completed them, he disliked the odour of his mouth and used a siwak (tooth-stick). The angels said: "We used to smell the scent of musk from you, and you spoiled it with the siwak." So God the Exalted commanded him to add ten more days to it.

It was also said that he was commanded to seclude himself for thirty [days] in fasting and worship, and then God sent down the Torah to him during the ten [days] and spoke to him in it.

﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron: Take my place among my people﴾: be my successor among them. ﴿And set things right﴾: [do] what must be set right in their affairs, or be a reformer. ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾: do not follow those who practise corruption, and do not obey whoever invites you to it.

It was also said that he was commanded to seclude himself for thirty [days] in fasting and worship, and then God sent down the Torah to him during the ten [days] and spoke to him in it.

﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron: Take my place among my people﴾: be my successor among them. ﴿And set things right﴾: [do] what must be set right in their affairs, or be a reformer. ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾: do not follow those who practise corruption, and do not obey whoever invites you to it.

﴿When Moses came at Our appointed time﴾ at the time We had set for him. The *lam* (ل) here indicates specificity (*ikhtisas*), meaning that his coming was specifically for Our appointed time. ﴿And his Lord spoke to him﴾ without an intermediary, as He speaks to the angels. It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, heard that speech from every direction, as an indication that hearing His eternal speech is not of the same kind as the speech of created beings.

﴿He said, "My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You."﴾ Show me Yourself, by enabling me to see You, or manifest Yourself to me so that I may look at You and see You. This is evidence that seeing God, may He be exalted, is permissible in general, for requesting the impossible from prophets is impossible, especially what would imply ignorance of God. For this reason He answered him with His words, exalted is He: ﴿"You will not see Me"﴾. He said *lan tarani* (لَنْ تَرانِي) rather than *lan ura* (لَنْ أُرى), *lan urika* (لَنْ أُرِيَكَ), or *lan tanzura ilayya* (لَنْ تَنْظُرَ إلَيَّ), to indicate that he was incapable of seeing Him, since seeing depends on a condition in the seer that had not yet been created in him. The question was asked in order to rebuke his people, who had said: ﴿"Show us God openly"﴾, and their statement was an error. For if seeing were impossible, He would have had to make them recognize their ignorance and remove their doubt, just as He did when they said: ﴿"Make for us a god"﴾, and He did not follow their path, as He said to his brother: ﴿"Do not follow the way of the corrupters"﴾. Deriving the impossibility of seeing from the answer is an even greater error, for the report that he was not seen does not indicate that He will never be seen, nor that no one else will ever see Him, let alone that it indicates impossibility. Claiming that it is self-evident (*darura*) in this matter is either arrogance or ignorance of the reality of seeing.

﴿He said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain. If it remains in its place, then you will see Me."﴾ This is a corrective exception (*istidrak*), intended to show that he could not bear it. Making the seeing conditional upon the mountain's remaining in its place also indicates permissibility, since what is conditional upon something possible is itself possible. It is said that the mountain was Mount Zubayr.

﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ His greatness appeared to it, and His power and command confronted it. It is also said that He gave it life and sight, so that it saw Him.

﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾ made it ground down and broken to pieces. *Dakk* (دَكّ) and *daqq* (دَقّ) are close in meaning, like *shakk* (شَكّ) and *shaqq* (شَقّ). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *dakka'* (دَكّاءَ), meaning a level ground, and from this comes the expression *naqa dakka'* (ناقَةٌ دَكّاءُ), a she-camel without a hump. It is also read *dakkan* (دَكًّا), meaning pieces, as the plural of *dakka'*.

﴿And Moses fell down unconscious (*sa'aqan*, صَعِقًا)﴾ senseless from the terror of what he had seen.

﴿Then when he regained consciousness, he said﴾ magnifying what he had seen: ﴿"Glory be to You! I repent to You"﴾ from the boldness and presumption of asking without permission. ﴿"And I am the first of the believers"﴾ its explanation has already passed. It is also said that its meaning is: I am the first to believe that You will not be seen in this world.

(p-34)﴿He said: "O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech.﴾ *iṣṭafaytuka*: I selected you. ﴿Above the people﴾: that is, those existing in your time. Hārūn, although he was a prophet, was commanded to follow him, and he was not a *kalīm* (one who was addressed directly by Allah) nor a bearer of a *sharīʿa* (a law-giving prophet). ﴿By My messages﴾: meaning the books (*asfār*) of the Tawrāt (Torah). Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ read *bi-risālatī* (in the singular). ﴿And by My speech﴾: and by My speaking to you directly. ﴿So take what I have given you﴾: what I have bestowed upon you of the message. ﴿And be among the grateful﴾: for the blessing it contains." It is narrated that the request to see [Allah] took place on the Day of ʿArafa, and the giving of the Torah took place on the Day of Nahr (the Day of Sacrifice).

﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning all things﴾: of what they need in matters of religion. ﴿An admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾: *mawʿiẓatan* is a substitute (*badal*) for the prepositional phrase *lahu* (for him), meaning: We wrote for him everything of admonitions and the detailed explanation of the rulings. It has been disputed whether the tablets were ten or seven in number, and whether they were of emerald (*zumurrud*), chrysolite (*zabarjad*), red ruby (*yāqūt aḥmar*), or a solid rock, which Allah softened for Mūsā, so that he cut it with his hand and smoothed it with his fingers. In them was the Torah or something else. ﴿So take them﴾: the verb is understood with an implied *qawl* (saying), coordinated with *katabnā* (We wrote), or it is a substitute (*badal*) for His saying ﴿So take what I have given you﴾. The pronoun *hā* (them) refers to the tablets, or to *kull shayʾ* (all things), since it has the meaning of *ashyāʾ* (things), or to the messages. ﴿With strength﴾: with earnestness and resolve.

﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾: that is, the best of what is in it, such as patience and pardon as opposed to retaliation and requital, in the manner of recommendation (*nadb*, a recommended act) and urging toward what is better, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Or [it means] its obligatory matters, since the obligatory is better than other things. It is also permissible that *al-aḥsan* (the best) is intended in an absolute sense of excellence, not in a comparative sense, and this is what is commanded, like their saying, "Summer is hotter than winter." ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: the abode of Pharaoh and his people in Egypt, lying in ruins upon their roofs, or the dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd and their likes, so that you may take warning and not transgress; or their abode in the Hereafter, which is Jahannam (Hell). It has been read *sa-ūrīkum* (I will make you see), meaning *sa-ubayyinu lakum* (I will make clear to you), from *awraytu al-zind* (I kindled the fire-stick); and *sa-ūrithukum* (I will make you inherit). This is supported by His saying: ﴿And We made the people inherit﴾.

Baydawi's Commentary (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah al-A'raf (7), verses 146–147:

﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ that are set up in the horizons and in themselves. ﴿Those who are arrogant﴾ on the earth, through the sealing of their hearts, so they do not reflect upon them or take warning from them. It has also been said: I will turn them away from refuting them, even if they strive to do so, as Pharaoh did, and it turned back upon him by their being raised up, or by their destruction. ﴿Without right﴾ is a complement (ṣila, the phrase completing the meaning of the verb) of "they are arrogant," meaning they are arrogant with what is not right, which is their false religion. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) referring to its doer. ﴿And if they see every sign﴾ that is sent down or a miracle. ﴿They will not believe in it﴾ because of their obstinacy and the disorder of their minds, caused by their immersion in desire and blind imitation. This supports the first interpretation. ﴿And if they see the path of right guidance, they will not take it as a path﴾ because Satanic influence has taken hold of them.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿al-rushd﴾ with two fatḥahs (ar-rushd), and it is also read as al-rashād. All three forms are dialectal variants, like al-suqm, al-saqam and al-saqām (illness). ﴿And if they see the path of error, they will take it as a path. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ That is, that turning away happens because of their denial and their failure to reflect upon the signs. It is also permissible for ﴿that﴾ to be in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: I will turn away that turning away because of these two things.

﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ meaning their meeting the Last Abode, or what Allah promised in the Last Abode.

﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ they gain nothing from them. ﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ meaning, except the recompense of their deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 148–149:

﴿And the people of Musa took, after him,﴾ after his departure for the appointed time (al-mīqāt). ﴿from their ornaments﴾ which they had borrowed from the Copts when they intended to leave Egypt. Their ornaments are attributed to them because they were in their possession, or because they came to own them after the Copts' destruction. It is the plural of ḥilī, like thudī and thady. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with a kasra, by assimilation (ittibā'), like dulī, and Ya'qub reads it in the singular. ﴿a calf, a body﴾ a body with flesh and blood, or a body of gold devoid of spirit, and it is put in the accusative as an apposition (badal). ﴿It had a lowing﴾ the sound of a cow.

It is narrated that when al-Sāmirī had fashioned the calf, he put into its mouth some dust from the hoofprint of Jibril's horse, and it became alive.

It is also said that he fashioned it with a kind of trick, so that the wind would enter its hollow and make it sound. The taking is attributed to them, though it was his act, either because they were content with it, or because what is meant is that they took it as a god. It was also read as juwār, meaning shouting. ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way?﴾ This is a rebuke for the extremity of their misguidance and their neglect of reflection. The meaning is: did they not see, when they took it as a god, that it has no power to speak or to guide to a path, as ordinary humans do, so that they supposed it was the creator of bodies, powers and decrees? ﴿They took it﴾ is a repetition for condemnation, meaning they took it as a god. ﴿And they were wrongdoers﴾ placing things in other than their proper places, so the taking of the calf was not an innovation (bid'a) unique to them.

﴿And when they regretted﴾ this is a metaphor for the intensity of their remorse, since the one who regrets and grieves bites his hand in distress, so that his hand is described as having fallen into it (maskūṭan fīhā). It is also read as saqata, in the active form, meaning that the biting fell upon it. It is also said that its meaning is that remorse fell upon their souls. ﴿And they saw﴾ and knew. ﴿that they had gone astray﴾ by taking the calf. ﴿They said: If our Lord does not have mercy on us﴾ by sending down the Torah, ﴿and forgive us﴾ by overlooking the sin, ﴿we will surely be among the losers.﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read both of these with the letter tā' (in the second person), and "our Lord" as a direct address (nidā').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 150–151:

﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾: "angry" (ghadban) meaning greatly wrathful; it is also said "grieved" (haznan). ﴿He said: "Evil is what you did after me"﴾: that is, what you did after me when you worshipped the calf. The address is to the worshippers, or it means: "You took my place and did not restrain the worshippers," and the address is to Harun and the believers with him. Ma (what) here is an indefinite noun described by a following clause (nakirah mawsufah), explaining the pronoun hidden in bi'sa (evil). The thing being censured is omitted; its estimated sense is: "Evil is the succession that you succeeded me in, your succession." The meaning of "after me" is after my departure, or after what you saw from me of monotheism (tawhid), glorification of God (tanzih), urging towards it, and restraining from what contradicts it. ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾: did you leave it incomplete? It is as if "hasten" (ajila) was used in the sense of "precede" (sabaqa), and so it took the same construction of transitivity; or the meaning is: "Did you hasten the promise of your Lord which He made to me of the forty (nights)," and you estimated my death and changed after me as the nations changed after their prophets. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾: he cast them down from the intensity of anger and the excess of vexation, out of zeal for the religion.

It is narrated: the Torah was in seven parts on seven tablets. When he threw them, they broke, so he lifted six parts of them, and in them was the detailed explanation of every thing, and one part remained, in which were the admonitions and the rulings.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾: by the hair of his head. ﴿Dragging him towards himself﴾: supposing that he had fallen short in restraining them. Harun was three years older than him, gentle and mild in temper, and for this reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel. ﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾: he mentioned the mother to soften him towards him, and they were of one father and one mother. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read here and in "Ta-Ha" "Ya ibna Ummi" with a kasrah. The original is "ya ibna ummiy," the ya was dropped, being sufficed by the kasrah, for lightness, like the vocative attached to the ya pronoun. The rest read with a fatha, as an added lightening because of its length, or by analogy with "khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen). ﴿Indeed the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me﴾: a clearing of the suspicion of shortcoming in his regard; the meaning is: I exerted my utmost in restraining them, until they overpowered me, deemed me weak, and came close to killing me. ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾: do not do to me what would cause them to gloat over me. ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾: do not count me among their number, by way of blame or attributing shortcoming.

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾: for what I did to my brother. ﴿And my brother﴾: if he fell short in restraining them, he joined him to himself in the seeking of forgiveness, to console him and to ward off gloating over him. ﴿And admit us into Your mercy﴾: by increasing favour upon us. ﴿And You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾: You are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves.

Ma (what) here is an indefinite noun described by a following clause (nakirah mawsufah), explaining the pronoun hidden in bi'sa (evil). The thing being censured is omitted; its estimated sense is: "Evil is the succession that you succeeded me in, your succession." The meaning of "after me" is after my departure, or after what you saw from me of monotheism (tawhid), glorification of God (tanzih), urging towards it, and restraining from what contradicts it. ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾: did you leave it incomplete? It is as if "hasten" (ajila) was used in the sense of "precede" (sabaqa), and so it took the same construction of transitivity; or the meaning is: "Did you hasten the promise of your Lord which He made to me of the forty (nights)," and you estimated my death and changed after me as the nations changed after their prophets. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾: he cast them down from the intensity of anger and the excess of vexation, out of zeal for the religion.

It is narrated: the Torah was in seven parts on seven tablets. When he threw them, they broke, so he lifted six parts of them, and in them was the detailed explanation of every thing, and one part remained, in which were the admonitions and the rulings.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾: by the hair of his head. ﴿Dragging him towards himself﴾: supposing that he had fallen short in restraining them. Harun was three years older than him, gentle and mild in temper, and for this reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel. ﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾: he mentioned the mother to soften him towards him, and they were of one father and one mother. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read here and in "Ta-Ha" "Ya ibna Ummi" with a kasrah. The original is "ya ibna ummiy," the ya was dropped, being sufficed by the kasrah, for lightness, like the vocative attached to the ya pronoun. The rest read with a fatha, as an added lightening because of its length, or by analogy with "khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen). ﴿Indeed the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me﴾: a clearing of the suspicion of shortcoming in his regard; the meaning is: I exerted my utmost in restraining them, until they overpowered me, deemed me weak, and came close to killing me. ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾: do not do to me what would cause them to gloat over me. ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾: do not count me among their number, by way of blame or attributing shortcoming.

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾: for what I did to my brother. ﴿And my brother﴾: if he fell short in restraining them, he joined him to himself in the seeking of forgiveness, to console him and to ward off gloating over him. ﴿And admit us into Your mercy﴾: by increasing favour upon us. ﴿And You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾: You are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 152–153:

﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [for worship] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord﴾. This is what He commanded them, namely killing themselves. ﴿And humiliation in the life of this world﴾. This is their departure from their homes. It was also said: it is the jizya (poll tax). ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ against Allah. There is no fabrication greater than their fabrication, which is their saying: "This is your god and the god of Musa." Perhaps no one before them or after them has fabricated the like of it.

﴿And those who committed evil deeds﴾ of disbelief and sins. ﴿Then repented after them﴾ after the evil deeds. ﴿And believed﴾ and devoted themselves to faith and what it requires of righteous deeds. ﴿Indeed, your Lord after them﴾ after the repentance. ﴿is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Even if the sin is great, like the crime of the calf-worshippers, and numerous, like the crimes of the Children of Israel.
