Even if the sin is great, like the crime of the calf-worshippers, and numerous, like the crimes of the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 154:

﴿And when the anger had subsided﴾ (sakana), and it has also been recited as ﴿sakata﴾. ﴿From Musa, the anger﴾ subsided through the apology of Harun, or through their repentance. In this statement there is emphasis and eloquence, in that he made the anger that moved him to what he did like one who commands him to it and urges him on, until he expressed its calming with the word "silence." It has also been recited as ﴿sakata﴾ and as ﴿askata﴾, on the basis that the one who silenced it is God, or his brother, or those who repented. ﴿He took up the tablets﴾ that he had thrown down. ﴿And in their copy﴾, and in what was copied (nuskha) in them, meaning written. It is the form fi'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like khutbah. It was also said: "what was copied from them," meaning from the broken tablets. ﴿Guidance﴾ is an explanation of the truth. ﴿And mercy﴾ is direction towards righteousness and good. ﴿For those who, for their Lord, are fearful﴾: the lam entered on the object because the verb is weakened by being placed later, or the object was omitted and the lam is for causation, and the implied sense is: they fear the disobedience of God for their Lord.

﴿Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment.﴾ That is, from among his people. The preposition is omitted and the verb is made to reach its object directly. ﴿Seventy men for Our appointment.﴾ The *mīqāt* (appointed time). ﴿So when the earthquake seized them.﴾ It is narrated that God commanded him to come to Him with seventy men from the Children of Israel. He chose six from each tribe, and two extra came forward. He said: "Let two of you remain behind," and they disputed. He said: "Indeed, for whoever stays behind is the reward of whoever goes out." So Kalib (Caleb) and Yusha' (Joshua) stayed behind, and the rest went with him. When they drew near the mountain, a cloud covered it, and Musa entered the cloud with them, and they fell down prostrate. They heard Him, exalted is He, speaking to Musa, commanding him and forbidding him. Then the cloud cleared, and they came to him and said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly.﴾ Then the earthquake seized them, that is, the thunderbolt (*sā'iqa*), or the trembling of the mountain, and they swooned from it. ﴿He said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me."﴾ He wished for their destruction and his own, either before he saw what he saw, or for another reason. Or he meant: You had power to destroy them before this, by driving Pharaoh to destroy them and to drown them in the sea and otherwise, and You showed mercy to them by rescuing them from that. So if You show them mercy a second time, it would not be far from Your abundant kindness. ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ Namely, from obstinacy and presumption in asking to see God. It is said that some of them said this. It is also said that what the foolish did refers to the worship of the calf, and that Musa chose the seventy for the appointed time of repentance from it. Then an awe overcame them (p-37), at which they became agitated and trembled until their joints nearly separated, and they were on the brink of destruction. Musa feared for them, so he wept and prayed, and God lifted it from them. ﴿It is none but Your trial.﴾ That is, Your testing, when You made them hear Your speech until they hoped to see You; or You created a lowing in the calf, and they went astray through it. ﴿By it You lead astray whom You will.﴾ Their misguidance is by transgressing its limit, or by following misleading appearances. ﴿And guide whom You will.﴾ Its guidance, so that his faith is strengthened by it. ﴿You are our Protector.﴾ The one who manages our affairs. ﴿So forgive us.﴾ By forgiving what we have committed. ﴿And have mercy on us, and You are the best of the forgivers.﴾ You forgive the evil deed and replace it with a good deed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 156:

﴿And prescribe for us in this world good,﴾ a good livelihood and success in obedience. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾ [prescribe good for us], [which is] Paradise. ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You.﴾ We have repented to You, from hada (ha-da), yahudu, meaning "to return." It is also read with a kasra (hidna), from hada yahidu-hu, meaning "to incline it," and it may be that the verb is active and passive in meaning: "we inclined ourselves" and "we were inclined to You." It is also permissible for the damma-vowelled form to be passive, from the dialect of those who say ʿawd al-marid (ʿūda al-marīḍ, "the sick man was visited").

﴿He said, "My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will,"﴾ [meaning] His punishing him. ﴿"And My mercy encompasses all things."﴾ In this world, the believer and the disbeliever, and indeed the obligated and others besides them, [are encompassed by it]. ﴿So I will write it﴾ — I will establish it in the Hereafter — or ﴿So I will write it﴾ as a special prescription for you, O Children of Israel.

﴿For those who fear﴾ disbelief and sins. ﴿And who give zakat﴾ — it is singled out for mention because of its excellence and because it was more burdensome for them. ﴿And those who believe in Our signs﴾ — so they do not disbelieve in any of them.

**Al-Baydawi's commentary (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah al-A'raf, verse 157:**

﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject, Arabic: مُبْتَدَأ), and its predicate (*khabar*, خَبَرُهُ) is ﴿He enjoins them﴾. Alternatively, it is the predicate of an implied subject, whose estimated form is ﴿They are those who﴾. Or it is a *badal* (substitute, بَدَلٌ) for ﴿those who fear﴾, either as a *badal al-ba'd* (partial substitute, بَدَلَ البَعْضِ) or as a *badal al-kull* (complete substitute, الكُلِّ). What is meant is those among them who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). He called him "Messenger" in relation to God, the Exalted, and "Prophet" in relation to the servants.

﴿the unlettered﴾ means the one who neither writes nor reads. He was described with this to draw attention to the fact that his complete knowledge, together with his state, is one of his miracles.

﴿whom they find written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ is both a name and a description.

﴿He enjoins them to do what is right and forbids them from what is wrong, and makes lawful for them the good things﴾, which had been forbidden to them, such as fats.

﴿and makes unlawful for them the bad things﴾, such as blood and the flesh of swine, or such as usury and bribery.

﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: he lightens for them the hard obligations that they had been charged with, such as prescribing retaliation (*qisas*, القصاص) for intentional and unintentional killing, cutting off the sinful limbs, and cutting away the place of impurity. The root of *al-isr* (إصْر) is a heavy load which *ya'sirus* (يَأْصِرُ) its bearer, meaning it confines him from movement because of its weight. Ibn 'Amir read *aşaraham* (آصارَهم) (in the plural form).

﴿So those who believed in him and honoured him﴾ means revered him by strengthening him. It has also been recited with the lighter form (*'azzarūhu*, عَزَّرُوهُ, read as *'azarūhu*), and its root meaning is to prevent, from which comes *ta'zir* (التَّعْزِيرُ, discretionary chastisement).

﴿and helped him﴾ for Me.

﴿and followed the light that was sent down with him﴾, meaning with his prophethood, namely the Qur'an. He called it a light because, by its inimitability, its matter is manifest and it makes other things manifest, or because it reveals the realities and makes them clear. It is also permissible for *ma'ahu* (مَعَهُ, "with him") to be connected to *ittaba'u* (اتَّبَعُوا, "followed"), meaning: they followed the light sent down together with following the Prophet. In that case it refers to following the Book and the Sunnah.

﴿Those are the ones who will prosper﴾, meaning those who attain eternal mercy. The meaning of the verse is the answer to the supplication of Musa (ﷺ).

(p-38) ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all."﴾ The address is general: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent to both jinn and humankind (al-thaqalan), whereas the other messengers were sent to their own peoples. ﴿Collectively (jami'an)﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "to you." ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a description (sifah) of Allah, even though it is separated from its referent by what is connected to the genitive noun, since that is like being placed before it. Alternatively, it is an accusative or nominative eulogy (madh), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿There is no god but Him﴾. These are the possibilities. The first (i.e., the description) serves to clarify what precedes it, for whoever possesses the world is the one God and none other. In ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ there is further affirmation of His exclusive right to divinity. ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His words﴾ refers to what was revealed to him and to the other messengers of His books and His revelation. It is also read as "wa-kalimatihi" (and His word), either to denote the category or to refer to the Qur'an, or to Jesus, as an allusion to the Jews and a warning that whoever does not believe in him, his faith is not considered valid. The shift from the first person to the third person is made in order to include these attributes which call to belief in him and following him. ﴿And follow him so that you may be guided﴾ makes the hope of being guided the result of the two commands, as an alert that whoever affirms him but does not follow him by adhering to his law is counted among the ranks of misguidance.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 159–160:

﴿And among the people of Musa﴾ meaning from the Children of Israel. ﴿a community who guide by the truth﴾ guiding people while being upright, or by a word of truth.

﴿And by it﴾ by the truth. ﴿they act justly﴾ among them in judgment. What is meant by them are those steadfast upon faith, standing by the truth from among the people of his time. He followed their mention with the mention of their opposites, as is the habit of the Qur'an, as an alert that the opposition of good and evil and the contention between the people of truth and falsehood is a continuing matter. It was also said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. It was also said: a people beyond China whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw on the night of the Mi'raj, and they believed in him.

﴿And We divided them﴾ and made them into separate groups, each distinguished from the others. ﴿into twelve﴾ is a second object of qattaʿa (qattaʿa, "to divide"), since it implies the meaning of ṣayyara (ṣayyara, "to make into"), or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). Its feminine form is due to agreement with ummah (ummah, "community") or qiṭʿah (qiṭʿah, "a portion"). ﴿tribes﴾ is a substitute for it, which is why it is plural, or it is a specifier (tamyīz) for it, on the basis that each one of the twelve is a tribe, so it is as if it were said: twelve tribes. It is also read with a kasra on the shīn and with it sukūn. ﴿nations﴾ according to the first reading is a substitute after a substitute, or an adjective of asbāṭ; and according to the second reading it is a substitute for asbāṭ.

﴿And We revealed to Musa, when his people asked him for water﴾ in the wilderness. ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ meaning he struck, and so it gushed forth. Its omission indicates that Musa (ﷺ) did not hesitate in carrying out the command, and that his striking was not an effective act upon which the event depended in itself. ﴿From it there gushed twelve springs; each people knew its drinking place﴾ each tribe. ﴿And We shaded them with clouds﴾ to shield them from the heat of the sun. ﴿And We sent down upon them manna and quails. "Eat"﴾ meaning and We said to them: eat. ﴿of the good things We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ its interpretation has already been explained in Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 161–162:

﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town"﴾ with the implied verb "remember" (idhkur) supplied; the town is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿And eat from it wherever you wish, and say "Hittah" and enter the gate prostrating﴾ has the same meaning as in Surah al-Baqarah, except that His saying ﴿so eat﴾ there with the fa' (fa, "so") indicates that their dwelling is the cause of eating from it. Here it is not mentioned, either being content with its mention there or because the context indicates it. As for the placing of His saying "say" before "enter," it has no effect on the meaning, because it does not necessitate sequence; likewise the conjunctive waw between them. ﴿We will forgive you your wrongs; We will increase the good-doers﴾ is a promise of forgiveness, and an increase upon it by reward. The second clause was expressed in the form of a new sentence (isti'naf) to indicate that it is pure bounty, not in exchange for what they were commanded. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read ﴿tughfar﴾ with the ta' and the passive form, and ﴿khati'atikum﴾ in the plural and nominative case, except Ibn 'Amir, who read it in the singular. Abu 'Amr read ﴿khatayakum﴾.

﴿But those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky because they were doing wrong﴾. Its explanation has already passed in it (in Surah al-Baqarah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 161–162:

﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town"﴾ with the implied verb "remember" (idhkur) supplied; the town is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿And eat from it wherever you wish, and say "Hittah" and enter the gate prostrating﴾ has the same meaning as in Surah al-Baqarah, except that His saying ﴿so eat﴾ there with the fa' (fa, "so") indicates that their dwelling is the cause of eating from it. Here it is not mentioned, either being content with its mention there or because the context indicates it. As for the placing of His saying "say" before "enter," it has no effect on the meaning, because it does not necessitate sequence; likewise the conjunctive waw between them. ﴿We will forgive you your wrongs; We will increase the good-doers﴾ is a promise of forgiveness, and an increase upon it by reward. The second clause was expressed in the form of a new sentence (isti'naf) to indicate that it is pure bounty, not in exchange for what they were commanded. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read ﴿tughfar﴾ with the ta' and the passive form, and ﴿khati'atikum﴾ in the plural and nominative case, except Ibn 'Amir, who read it in the singular. Abu 'Amr read ﴿khatayakum﴾.

﴿But those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky because they were doing wrong﴾. Its explanation has already passed in it (in Surah al-Baqarah).

﴿And ask them﴾ for confirmation and rebuke, regarding their long-standing disbelief and disobedience, and to inform you of what is among their knowledge that cannot be known except through instruction or revelation, so that this would be a miracle for you against them. ﴿About the town﴾ about its news and what befell its people. ﴿Which was by the sea﴾ near it. It was Aylah, a town between Madyan and Tur on the seashore. It was also said to be Madyan, and it was said to be Tiberias. ﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ they overstepped God's limits by hunting on the Sabbath day. ﴿Idh﴾ (when) is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) governing ﴿كانت﴾ (was) or ﴿حاضرة﴾ (near), or governing an omitted noun, or it is a substitute (badal ishtimal, a substitution of inclusion) for that omitted noun. ﴿When their fish came to them﴾ is an adverbial of time governing ﴿يعدون﴾ (they transgress), or a substitute following another substitute. It was also read as ﴿يَعْدُونَ﴾ with the root ﻳَعْتَدُونَ (ya'tadūn, they transgress), or ﻳُعِدُّونَ (yu'iddūn) from iʿdād (preparation), meaning they prepare the tools of hunting on the Sabbath day, although they had been forbidden to occupy themselves on it with anything other than worship. ﴿On their Sabbath day, appearing openly﴾ on the day when they magnified the matter of the Sabbath. Sabbatat (the verb) is the verbal noun of ﻣَصْدَرُ سَبَتَتِ اليَهُودُ (the Jews observed the Sabbath), when they magnified their Sabbath by devoting themselves to worship. It was also said that "Sabt" is the name of the day, and the idafa (construction of possession) is because they were singled out for rulings concerning it. The first view is supported by the reading ﻳَوْمَ إسْباتِهِمْ (yawm isbātihim, the day of their observing the Sabbath), and by His saying: ﴿and on the day they do not keep the Sabbath, they will not come to them﴾. It was also read as ﻻ يَسْبِتُونَ (lā yasbitūn, from asbata) and as ﻻ يُسْبِتُونَ (lā yusbitūn), in the passive form, meaning they do not enter upon the Sabbath. ﴿Shurraʿan﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the fish, and its meaning is apparent on the surface of the water, from shara'a ʿalaynā (it approached us) when it drew near and came into view. ﴿Thus We tested them for what they used to defiantly disobey﴾ with a trial of similar severity, We tested them because of their disobedience. It was also said that "thus" is connected to what precedes it, meaning: they do not come to them in the same manner as their coming on the Sabbath day, and the bāʾ (with) is related to ﴿يعدون﴾ (they transgress).

And when a community among them said: "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy, or punish with a severe punishment?" This is conjoined with "when they transgressed the Sabbath" (idh ya'dūna). "A community among them" refers to a group of the people of the town, namely their righteous ones, who had striven hard in admonishing them until they despaired of their taking heed. "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy" means: whom He is going to annihilate (mukhtarimuhum). "Or punish with a severe punishment" means in the Hereafter, because of their persistence in disobedience. They said this as an exaggeration of the point that admonition is of no benefit to them. Or it is a question about the purpose of admonition and its benefit, as if it were a mutual dispute among them, or the words of one who had given up admonishing those among them who would not give up (their transgression). It was also said that the intended group is a faction from the doomed sect who answered their admonishers with this, rebutting them and mocking them.

They said: "As an excuse to your Lord" (ma'dhiratan ilā rabbikum). This is the answer to the question, meaning: our admonition is the discharge of an excuse before Allah, so that we will not be blamed for negligence in forbidding the evil. Ḥafs read ma'dhiratan with the accusative, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as a purpose clause (ʿillah), meaning: we offered this as an excuse, and we admonished them as an excuse.

"And perhaps they will become God-fearing" (wa-laʿallahum yattaqūn), since despair does not arise except through destruction.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 165–166:

﴿When they forgot﴾ means they abandoned it in the manner of one who has forgotten. ﴿what they had been reminded of﴾ means what their righteous ones (ṣulaḥā'uhum) had reminded them of. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong﴾ with transgression and opposition to God's command. ﴿with a severe punishment (ʿadhāb baʾīs)﴾ meaning severe. It is the form faʿīl from بَؤُسَ yabʾusu buʾsan, meaning "it became intense" (ishtadda). Abu Bakr read (بَيْئَسٍ) on the pattern fayʿal, like ḍaygham. Ibn ʿAmir read « بِئْسٍ » with a kasra on the bāʾ and a sukūn on the hamza, as if it were بَئِسَ on the pattern ḥadhira. This reading is also attested, and its ʿayn was lightened by moving its vowel to the fāʾ, as in kabud for kabid. Nafiʿ read « بَيِسَ » either by changing the hamza into a yāʾ, as it was changed in dhiʾb, or taking it as a verb of blame that was used as a noun. It was also read « بَيِّسٍ » like rayyis, by changing the hamza and then assimilating it. « بَيِّسٍ » with light stress is like hayyin, and « بائِسٍ » is like fāʿil. ﴿because they were defiantly disobedient﴾ means because of their wickedness.

﴿When they defied what they had been forbidden﴾ means they became arrogant in refusing to abandon what they had been forbidden, as in His saying, ﴿and they defied the command of their Lord﴾. ﴿We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ is like His saying, ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. The apparent meaning requires that God first punished them with a severe punishment, and then they defied, after which He transformed them. It is also possible that the second verse is a confirmation and elaboration of the first.

It is narrated that when those who forbade (evil) despaired of the transgressors heeding admonition, they disliked living alongside them. So they divided the town with a wall that had a door, which was kept closed. One morning none of the transgressors came out to them, so they said, "Something has happened to them," and they entered upon them, and behold, they were apes. They did not recognize their relatives, but the apes recognized them. They came to their relatives, sniffed their clothes, and went around them weeping. Then they died after three days.

It is also narrated from Mujahid that their hearts were transformed, not their bodies.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 167–168:

﴿And when your Lord declared﴾: that is, He made known (a'lama), from the form tafa''ala derived from al-iydhan (making known), with the same meaning as al-tawa''ud and al-i'ad (threatening and promising). Or it means He resolved (azama), because one who resolves upon a thing makes himself aware of doing it. It is treated as the function of an oath, like ﴿Allah knows﴾ and ﴿Allah bears witness﴾. For this reason it is answered with its answer, which is: ﴿He will surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection﴾. The meaning is: "And when your Lord made it binding upon Himself that He would surely impose upon the Jews" ﴿those who would inflict on them the worst torment﴾, such as humiliation and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). After Sulayman (peace be upon him), Allah sent against them Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), who ruined their dwellings, killed their fighting men, took their women and offspring captive, and imposed the jizya on those of them who remained. They used to pay it to the Magians, until Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), and he did what he did, and then imposed the jizya upon them, so it continues to be imposed until the end of time. ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾: He punished them in this world. ﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward whoever repents and believes.

﴿And We divided them in the earth into communities﴾: We scattered them throughout it, such that hardly any region is free of them, as a means of cutting off their backs, so that they never have any power at all. ﴿Communities﴾ is a second object or a circumstantial accusative (hal). ﴿Among them are the righteous﴾: this is an attribute or a substitute for "them". They are those who believed in Medina and their counterparts. ﴿And among them are others below that﴾: its estimate is "and among them are people other than that", that is, those lowered from righteousness, and they are their disbelievers and transgressors. ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾: with blessings and afflictions. ﴿That perhaps they would return﴾: they would be admonished, so they would turn back from what they were upon.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 169–170:

﴿Then there succeeded them﴾ after those mentioned. ﴿Successors (khalf)﴾ is a substitute for evil. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective, which is why it applies to both the singular and the plural. It is also said to be a plural, and it is commonly used for evil, whereas khalaf with a fatḥa is used for good. The intended are those who were in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who inherited the Book, the Torah, from their forefathers, reading it and understanding what is in it. . . ﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾ the trash of this lowly thing, meaning the world. It is derived from nearness (duww) or baseness (danā'a), and it refers to what they used to take as bribes in judgment and for distorting the words. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw (of the subject). ﴿And they say: "It will be forgiven us"﴾ God will not hold us accountable for that and will overlook it. This may be read as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) or as a circumstantial clause, and the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase, or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ﴿they take﴾. ﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾ this is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿for us﴾, meaning: they hope for forgiveness while persisting in sin, returning to its like, not repenting of it. ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾ that is, in the Book. ﴿That they would not say about God except the truth﴾ this is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to the covenant, or it is connected to it, meaning: that they would say. The purpose is to rebuke them for affirming forgiveness while not repenting, and the indication that this is a fabrication against God and a departure from the covenant of the Book. ﴿And they studied what is in it﴾ it is conjoined with ﴿Was not ... taken﴾ in meaning, since it is an affirmation, or it is conjoined with ﴿inherited﴾, and this is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). ﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who are mindful of God﴾ than what these people take. ﴿Will you not then use your reason﴾ so that they would know this and not exchange the lower, base thing, which leads to punishment, for the everlasting bliss. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ and Yaʿqūb read it with the letter tāʾ, by way of shift (of address) (talwīn). ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer﴾ this is conjoined to ﴿those who are mindful of God﴾. The statement ﴿Will you not then use your reason﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ), or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is: ﴿Indeed We do not waste the reward of the reformers﴾, with the implied ﴿of them﴾, or the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to alert that reform acts as a safeguard against waste. Abū Bakr read ﴿hold fast﴾ with the lightened form, and the singular ﴿establish﴾, because it is more excellent than all other kinds of holding fast.

﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾, i.e., We uprooted it and lifted it above them. The root meaning of *naṭq* is pulling.

﴿as if it were a canopy﴾: a shelter, i.e., anything that shades you from above.

﴿And they thought﴾, i.e., and were certain,

﴿that it would fall upon them﴾, i.e., drop onto them. This is because a mountain does not stay suspended in the air, and because they had been warned of it. He used the word *ẓann* (thought) because its object had not yet occurred. The reason they were threatened was that they refused to accept the rulings of the Tawrah (Torah) because of their weight, so God raised the Ṭūr (Mount Sinai) above them.

It was said to them: if you accept what is in it, well and good; otherwise it will certainly fall upon you.

﴿Take﴾ is in the imperative, governed by an implied verb of saying (*iḍmār al-qawl*, an unstated verb of speech). The sense is: "And We said, 'Take…'" or "saying, 'Take…'"

﴿what We have given you﴾, i.e., of the Scripture,

﴿with strength﴾, i.e., with earnestness and resolve to bear its hardships. This is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) relating to the *wāw* in *khudhū* (the plural pronoun of the verb, i.e., "you" in "take").

﴿and remember what is in it﴾, i.e., by acting upon it, and do not neglect it as one who has forgotten.

﴿so that you may be righteous﴾, i.e., avoid ugly deeds and base moral qualities.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verses 172–174:

﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ That is, He brought forth from their loins their progeny, generation after generation, as they reproduce. "From their loins" (*min zuhurihim*) is a substitution (*badal*) for "the Children of Adam," a substitution of part for whole. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read *"dhurriyyatihim"* (their offspring, in the plural form *dhurriyyat*). ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ That is, He set up for them the proofs of His lordship and placed in their intellects what calls them to acknowledge it, until they became as though it had been said to them, "Am I not your Lord?" and they had answered, "Yes." Their being enabled to know Him, and their capacity to do so, took the place of testimony and acknowledgment, by way of figurative expression (*tamthil*). This is indicated by His saying: ﴿lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, lest you should say it. ﴿"Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾, that is, we were not alerted to it by any proof.

﴿Or you should say﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with ﴿lest you should say﴾. Abu 'Amr read both verbs with the *ya'* (third person), because the beginning of the discourse is in the third person (*al-ghaybah*). ﴿"It was only that our forefathers associated partners with God before, and we were offspring after them﴾, so we followed them. For blind imitation (*taqlid*) is not an acceptable excuse when proof has been established and one is able to acquire knowledge of it. ﴿"Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾, meaning their forefathers, the falsifiers, who founded polytheism. It has also been said that when God created Adam, He brought forth from his back offspring like specks (*kal-dharr*), gave them life, made them intellect and speech, and inspired them with that, based on a hadith related by 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). I have verified the discussion of this in my commentary on the book *al-Masabih*. The purpose of mentioning this statement here is to hold the Jews accountable to the requirements of the general covenant (*al-mithaq al-'amm*), after having held them accountable to the covenant specific to them, and to argue against them with both transmitted and rational proofs, and to forbid them from blind imitation (*taqlid*) and to direct them toward reflection and reasoning (*istidlal*), as He said: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, so that perhaps they may return﴾, that is, from blind imitation and following falsehood. (p-42)

(p-42)

﴿And recite to them﴾, that is, to the Jews, ﴿the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾. He is one of the scholars of the Children of Israel (Banu Isra'il), or he is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, for he had read the books and knew that God, exalted is He, would send a messenger in that age, and he hoped that he himself would be that messenger. But when Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent, he envied him and disbelieved in him. Or he is Bal'am ibn Ba'ura' of the Canaanites, who was given knowledge of some of God's books. ﴿Then he detached himself from them﴾, from the signs, by disbelieving in them and turning away from them. ﴿So Satan pursued him﴾, until he overtook him; it is also said that he made him follow him. ﴿And he became of the misguided﴾, that is, he became one of the astray.

It is narrated that his people asked him to invoke curses upon Musa and those who were with him. He said: "How can I invoke a curse upon one who is accompanied by the angels?" They pressed him until he invoked a curse against them, and so they remained in the wandering (al-tih, the desert wandering).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 176–177:

﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him﴾ to the ranks of the righteous among the scholars. ﴿by them﴾, by means of those verses and by adhering to them. ﴿But he inclined toward the earth﴾, he leaned toward this world, or toward baseness. ﴿And followed his desire﴾ by preferring this world and seeking the approval of his people, and he turned away from what the verses required. He attached his elevation to the will of God, Exalted is He, and then corrected this by the act of the servant. This is to draw attention to the fact that the will is the cause of his act, which necessitates his elevation, and that its absence is evidence of its absence, in the way that the absence of an effect indicates the absence of its cause. It also shows that the true cause is the will, and that what we observe of causes are intermediaries that are considered in bringing about the effect, insofar as the will has been directed toward them in this way. It would have been proper for him to say, "But he turned away from them," so he placed in its position ﴿inclined toward the earth and followed his desire﴾, for emphasis and to draw attention to what drove him to it, and that love of this world is the root of every sin. ﴿So his likeness﴾, i.e., his description, which is a figure of speech for baseness, ﴿is like the likeness of the dog﴾, like its description in its most despicable state, which is ﴿if you drive it away, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾, meaning it pants constantly, whether it is driven away with rebuke and chasing or left alone without being disturbed, unlike the rest of the animals, because of the weakness of its heart. Al-lahth (panting) is the protrusion of the tongue from intense breathing. The conditional clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is: panting in both states. The comparison stands in the place of the necessary consequence of the structure, which is the negation of elevation, and the placing of him in a lowly rank is for emphasis and clarification. It has been said that when he (ﷺ) supplicated against Musa (ﷺ), his tongue came out and fell upon his chest, and he began to pant like a dog. ﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories﴾, the story mentioned, to the Jews, for it is similar to their stories, ﴿that perhaps they may reflect﴾, a reflection that leads them to be admonished.

﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾, i.e., the likeness of the people is evil. It is also read as (ساءَ مَثَلُ القَوْمِ), with the object of blame omitted. ﴿who denied Our signs﴾ after the proof had been established against them and they had knowledge of them. ﴿And they used to wrong themselves﴾. This may be part of the relative clause, conjoined with "denied," in the sense of: those who combined the denial of the signs with wronging themselves; or it may be disjoined from it, in the sense of: they did not wrong anyone by denying, except themselves, for its harm does not go beyond them, and for this reason the object was placed first.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 176–177:

﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him﴾ to the ranks of the righteous among the scholars. ﴿by them﴾, by means of those verses and by adhering to them. ﴿But he inclined toward the earth﴾, he leaned toward this world, or toward baseness. ﴿And followed his desire﴾ by preferring this world and seeking the approval of his people, and he turned away from what the verses required. He attached his elevation to the will of God, Exalted is He, and then corrected this by the act of the servant. This is to draw attention to the fact that the will is the cause of his act, which necessitates his elevation, and that its absence is evidence of its absence, in the way that the absence of an effect indicates the absence of its cause. It also shows that the true cause is the will, and that what we observe of causes are intermediaries that are considered in bringing about the effect, insofar as the will has been directed toward them in this way. It would have been proper for him to say, "But he turned away from them," so he placed in its position ﴿inclined toward the earth and followed his desire﴾, for emphasis and to draw attention to what drove him to it, and that love of this world is the root of every sin. ﴿So his likeness﴾, i.e., his description, which is a figure of speech for baseness, ﴿is like the likeness of the dog﴾, like its description in its most despicable state, which is ﴿if you drive it away, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾, meaning it pants constantly, whether it is driven away with rebuke and chasing or left alone without being disturbed, unlike the rest of the animals, because of the weakness of its heart. Al-lahth (panting) is the protrusion of the tongue from intense breathing. The conditional clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is: panting in both states. The comparison stands in the place of the necessary consequence of the structure, which is the negation of elevation, and the placing of him in a lowly rank is for emphasis and clarification. It has been said that when he (ﷺ) supplicated against Musa (ﷺ), his tongue came out and fell upon his chest, and he began to pant like a dog. ﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories﴾, the story mentioned, to the Jews, for it is similar to their stories, ﴿that perhaps they may reflect﴾, a reflection that leads them to be admonished.

﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾, i.e., the likeness of the people is evil. It is also read as (ساءَ مَثَلُ القَوْمِ), with the object of blame omitted. ﴿who denied Our signs﴾ after the proof had been established against them and they had knowledge of them. ﴿And they used to wrong themselves﴾. This may be part of the relative clause, conjoined with "denied," in the sense of: those who combined the denial of the signs with wronging themselves; or it may be disjoined from it, in the sense of: they did not wrong anyone by denying, except themselves, for its harm does not go beyond them, and for this reason the object was placed first.

(p-43) ﴿Whoever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whoever He leads astray, it is they who are the losers.﴾ This is an explicit statement that guidance and misguidance are from Allah, that Allah's guidance is specific to some and not others, and that it necessitates being guided. The singular in the first clause and the plural in the second are according to the wording (lafz): the meaning is a notice that the guided are like one person because their path is unified, unlike the misguided. Limiting the report about the one whom Allah has guided to "the guided one" is a magnification of the status of guidance, and a notice that it is in itself a great perfection and a mighty benefit; even if nothing else were attained, it would suffice, and it is that which necessitates success in the everlasting blessings and is the sign of them.

﴿And We have certainly created﴾ (dhara'na) means: We created. ﴿For Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾ meaning those who persist in disbelief in His knowledge, may He be exalted.

﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ since they do not direct them toward knowing the truth and reflecting upon its proofs. ﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see﴾ i.e., they do not look at what Allah has created with the look of consideration (i'tibar). ﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ the verses and admonitions with the hearing of contemplation and remembrance.

﴿Those are like cattle﴾ in lacking understanding and sight for consideration and hearing for reflection; or in that their senses and faculties are directed toward the means of livelihood and confined to them. ﴿Nay, they are even more astray﴾ for cattle perceive what they are able to perceive of benefits and harms, and strive with their utmost effort to attract them and avert them, whereas they are not like that; rather most of them know that they are obstinate, yet they proceed into the Fire. ﴿Those are the heedless﴾, the perfect in heedlessness.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 7, verses 180–181:**

﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾, because they signify meanings that are the most beautiful of meanings. What is meant by them is the words, though it has been said that it means the attributes.

﴿So call upon Him by them﴾, that is, name Him by those names. ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾, that is, abandon naming those who go astray concerning them, who call Him by what has no tawqif (textual authorization from revelation) behind it, since it may suggest a corrupt meaning, such as their saying "O Father of Generosity" or "O White-Faced One." Or, do not concern yourselves with their denial of what He named Himself by, such as their saying, "We do not know any Raḥmān except the Raḥmān of Yamamah." Or, it means: leave them and their deviation concerning them, by applying them to idols and deriving the names of those idols from them, like al-Lat from "Allah" and al-'Uzza from "al-'Aziz." Do not agree with them in this, or turn away from them, for Allah will requite them, as He said: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾. Hamzah read ﴿yulhidūn﴾ here and in "Fussilat" with a fatha, and it is said that laḥada and alḥada mean to deviate from the right course.

﴿And among those We have created is a community that guides by the truth and acts justly by it﴾. He mentioned this after He had explained that He created for the Fire a group who go astray and deviate from the truth, to indicate that He also created for Paradise a community who guide by the truth and are just in the matter. This verse has been cited as evidence for the validity of ijma' (scholarly consensus), because what is meant by it is that in every generation (qarn) there is a group with this attribute, based on his statement, may blessings and peace be upon him: "A group of my Ummah will continue to be upon the truth until the command of Allah comes." For if it were restricted to the time of the Messenger or to another specific period, there would be no benefit in it, since that is already known.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 182–184:

﴿And those who deny Our signs – We will draw them on step by step﴾ We will bring them closer to destruction little by little. The root of istidraj (gradual drawing-on, leading step by step) is either ascending or descending, one degree after another. ﴿From where they do not know﴾ what We intend for them. This is that blessings will follow one upon another for them, so they think they are a kindness from God Most High toward them, and they increase in insolence and immersion in error until the word of punishment is justly due against them.

﴿And I will give them respite﴾ and grant them time, joined to ﴿We will draw them on step by step﴾. ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾ indeed, My seizing is severe. He called it a plan (kayd) because its outward appearance is kindness while its inward reality is abandonment.

﴿Do they not reflect? There is no madness in their companion﴾ meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Madness (jinnah)﴾ means insanity.

It is narrated: "He (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa and called them clan by clan, warning them of the punishment of God Most High. One of them said: 'Your companion is truly mad; he spent the night raving until morning.' Then this was revealed." ﴿He is only a clear warner﴾ his warning is evident, such that it is not hidden from any observer.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 185–186:

﴿Have they not considered﴾ with the consideration of inference (nazar istidlal) ﴿into the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth and whatever thing Allah has created﴾ of the kinds that fall under the name "thing" and which cannot be enumerated, so that it may indicate to them the perfection of the power of its Maker, the oneness of its Originator, and the greatness of the station of its Owner and the one who governs its affairs, so that He may show them the soundness of what He calls them to. ﴿And that it may be that their term has drawn near﴾ is coordinated with "dominion"; "that" (an) is either verbal (masdariyya) or the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy, its noun being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and likewise the noun of "may be" (yakun). The meaning is: have they not considered the drawing near of their terms and the expectation of their arrival, so that they would hasten to seek the truth and turn to what saves them, before the sudden seizure of death and the descent of punishment. ﴿Then in what statement after this﴾ means after the Qur'an. ﴿will they believe?﴾ if they do not believe in it. This is the utmost in clarification, as if it were a report about them of their natural disposition and determination upon disbelief after the establishment of proof and the guidance to reflection. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying "it may be that it has drawn near," as if it were said: perhaps their term has drawn near, so why do they not hasten to believe in the Qur'an, and what are they waiting for after its clarity? If they do not believe in it, then in what statement more worthy than it do they wish to believe?

As for His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him﴾, it serves as an affirmation and a causal explanation of it. ﴿And He leaves them in their transgression﴾ is in the nominative as a resumption (isti'naf). Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with the "ya" (yadharuhum), in agreement with His saying "whomever Allah leaves astray." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the "ya" and with the jussive, coordinating it with the position (mahall) of ﴿there is no guide for him﴾, as if it were said: no one guides him besides Him, ﴿and He leaves them﴾. ﴿Wandering blindly﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "them."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 7, verse 187:**

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾ That is, about the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It is one of the predominant names (al-asma' al-ghalibah) for it, and it is applied to it either because it occurs suddenly, or because its reckoning is swift, or because, despite its length, it is with God like an hour. ﴿Its appointed time (ayyana mursaha)﴾: when is its anchoring (irsa'uha), that is, its establishment and settling. Ruww al-shay' means its firmness and settling, and from it come *rasa al-jabal* (the mountain became firmly fixed) and *arsa al-safinah* (he anchored the ship). The derivation of *ayyan* is from *ayy*, because its meaning is "which time," and it is from *awaytu ilayhi* (I took refuge with him), because the part gathers around the whole. ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord.﴾ He has kept it exclusively to Himself; He has not revealed it to any honoured angel or any sent prophet. ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time.﴾ That is, He will not manifest its matter at its time. ﴿None but He﴾: the meaning is that its concealment continues for everyone else until the time of its occurrence. The *lam* here indicates a time limit, like the *lam* in His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. ﴿It has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾: it has become great for their inhabitants, from among the angels and the two species (humans and jinn), because of its terror. This seems to be an indication of the wisdom in concealing it. ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾: only abruptly, while you are heedless, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "The Hour will come upon people while a man is repairing his pool, and a man is watering his livestock, and a man is displaying his merchandise in his market, and a man is lowering his scale and raising it."

﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾: knowing it. *Hafiyy* is an intensive form (fa'il) from *hafiya 'an al-shay'*, meaning he asked about it. Whoever questions a matter thoroughly and searches into it has firmly established knowledge of it, and for this reason it is followed by *'an*. It has also been said that *yas'alunaka* is the complement of this phrase. It has also been said that it derives from *al-hafawah* in the sense of compassion, because the Quraysh said to him: "There is kinship between us and you, so tell us when the Hour will be." The meaning is: they ask you about it as though you were being solicitous toward them, so you single them out, because of their kinship, by teaching them its time. It has also been said that the meaning is: as though you were eager about asking about it, which you love, from *hafiya bi'l-shay'* when one is delighted with something, that is, you repeat it often, because it is among the unseen matters that God has kept exclusively to His own knowledge. ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with God﴾: He repeated it because of the repetition of *yas'alunaka*, due to the additional element attached to it, and for emphasis. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that its knowledge is with God and that He has not granted it to anyone of His creation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 188:

﴿Say: I possess not for myself any benefit or harm﴾ — that is, bringing about benefit or warding off harm. This is a display of servitude (ʿubudiyyah) and a disavowal of any claim to knowledge of the unseen (ghuyub). ﴿Except what Allah wills﴾ of that, so that He inspires me with it and grants me success in it. ﴿And had I known the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good, and no evil would have touched me﴾ — that is, had I known it, I would have changed my state from what it is, by acquiring abundant benefits and avoiding harms, so that no evil would touch me. ﴿I am but a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ — that is, I am only a servant sent for warning and giving good tidings. ﴿For a people who believe﴾ — for it is they who benefit from both of them. It is also permissible for this to be related to ﴿bringer of good tidings﴾, while the object of ﴿warner﴾ is omitted.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 189:**

﴿It is He who created you from a single soul.﴾ This is Adam. ﴿And made from it﴾ from its body, from one of its ribs, or from its own kind, as in His saying: ﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves.﴾ ﴿Its mate﴾ Eve. ﴿So that he might find rest in her﴾ that he might find companionship and tranquility with her, the tranquility of a thing with its part or its kind. The pronoun is masculine here because the sense is taken into account, for the sake of harmony. ﴿When he covered her﴾ that is, had intercourse with her.

﴿She bore a light burden﴾ it was light for her, and she did not suffer from it the harm that pregnant women usually suffer. Or it means she carried a light load, namely the sperm-drop. ﴿And she went about with it﴾ she continued with it, that is, she stood and sat. It is also read as *famarrat* (with the verb unstressed) and as *fastamarrat bihi*, and as *famarat* from *al-mawr*, which means coming and going. Or it is from *al-miryah* (doubt), meaning she supposed it to be a pregnancy and had doubts about it. ﴿When she grew heavy﴾ she became heavy with the great size of the child in her womb. It is also read in the passive form, meaning her pregnancy made her heavy. ﴿They both called upon God, their Lord: "If You give us a righteous one"﴾ a child who is sound, whose body is healthy. ﴿We will surely be among the thankful﴾ to You for this renewed blessing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 190–191:

﴿So when He gave them a righteous child, they ascribed to Him partners in what He had given them.﴾ That is, their children became partners to Him in what He had given their children. They named the child ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā and ʿAbd Manāf, by omitting a noun (muḍāf) and placing the noun it is attached to (muḍāf ilayhi) in its position. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾

﴿Do they associate with Him that which creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ This refers to the idols. It is also said: when Ḥawwāʾ conceived, Iblīs came to her in the form of a man and said to her: "What do you know of what is in your womb? Perhaps it is an animal or a dog. And what do you know of how it will come out?" She feared this and mentioned it to Ādam, who understood it from him. Then he returned to her and said: "I have a station with Allah; if I pray to Allah that He make it a creature like you and ease its coming out for you, will you name him ʿAbd al-Ḥārith?" His name among the angels was Ḥārith, so she accepted. When she gave birth, they named him ʿAbd al-Ḥārith.

Such things are not fitting for the prophets. It is also possible that the address in ﴿He created you﴾ is to the family of Quṣayy from Quraysh, for they were created from the self of Quṣayy, and he had a spouse of his own kind, an Arab Qurashiyya. They asked Allah for a child, and He gave them four sons, whom they named: ʿAbd Manāf, ʿAbd Shams, ʿAbd Quṣayy, and ʿAbd al-Dār. In that case the pronoun in ﴿they associate﴾ refers to the two of them and to their descendants who followed them. Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr read "shirkan" (شِرْكًا), meaning a sharing, in that they made others share in it; or [it means] possessors of a share, and they are the partners (al-shurakāʾ), and the pronoun "they" refers to the idols, brought in on account of their naming them gods.

His name among the angels was Ḥārith, so she accepted. When she gave birth, they named him ʿAbd al-Ḥārith.

Such things are not fitting for the prophets. It is also possible that the address in ﴿He created you﴾ is to the family of Quṣayy from Quraysh, for they were created from the self of Quṣayy, and he had a spouse of his own kind, an Arab Qurashiyya. They asked Allah for a child, and He gave them four sons, whom they named: ʿAbd Manāf, ʿAbd Shams, ʿAbd Quṣayy, and ʿAbd al-Dār. In that case the pronoun in ﴿they associate﴾ refers to the two of them and to their descendants who followed them. Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr read "shirkan" (شِرْكًا), meaning a sharing, in that they made others share in it; or [it means] possessors of a share, and they are the partners (al-shurakāʾ), and the pronoun "they" refers to the idols, brought in on account of their naming them gods.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 192–193:

(p-46) ﴿And they are not able to help them (لَهم نَصْرًا)﴾, i.e., their worshippers. ﴿Nor can they help themselves﴾, so as to repel from themselves what befalls them.

﴿And if you call them﴾, i.e., the polytheists, ﴿to guidance﴾, i.e., to Islam, ﴿they will not follow you﴾. Nafi' recited it with the lightened form and an open ba' (yattabi'uukum → *yatba'ukum*, i.e., lā yatba‘ūkum). It was also said that the address is to the polytheists, and the pronoun (hum) refers to the idols, meaning: if you call them (the idols) to guide you, they will not follow you to your desire, nor will they answer you as Allah answers you. ﴿It is all the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾. He did not say "am ṣamattum" (or you were silent) for emphasis on the fact that calling them yields no benefit, since their state is equated with constant silence; or because they did not call upon them for their needs, so it is as if it was said: it is all the same for you whether you begin calling them or continue in silence from calling upon them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 194–195:

﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾ means: those whom you worship and name as gods. ﴿are servants like you﴾ in that they are owned and subjugated. ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful﴾ that they are gods. It is possible that when they carved them in the forms of humans, He said to them: At most, their state is that they are living, rational beings like you, so they do not deserve your worship, just as some of you do not deserve the worship of others. Then He turned against it with a refutation, saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or do they have hands with which they strike, or do they have eyes with which they see, or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ It is also read "Inna alladhina" with the "inna" lightened and "ibad" in the accusative, taking the particle as a negation that functions like the Hijazi "ma," though no such usage is established otherwise; and "yubtishuna" is read with a damma here, and in "al-Qasas" and "al-Dukhan." ﴿Say: Call upon your associates﴾ and seek their help against me. ﴿Then plot against me﴾ so exhaust in whatever scheming you are able to do, you and your associates. ﴿And do not give me respite﴾ do not delay me. For indeed I am not concerned with you, because of my reliance upon the guardianship and protection of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 196–198:

﴿Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who sent down the Book﴾, i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿And He takes charge of the righteous﴾, meaning: it is among His habits, exalted is He, to take charge of the righteous among His servants, let alone His prophets.

﴿And those you call upon besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves﴾ is part of the justification for His not caring about them.

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear; and you see them looking at you, but they do not see﴾: they resemble those who look at you, because they have been depicted in the form of one who looks at someone facing him.

﴿Take forgiveness﴾, that is, take what comes to you easily from people's actions, and do not demand what is burdensome for them, from *al-ʿafw* (forgiveness, ease), which is the opposite of effort (*al-juhd*). Or it means: take forgiveness toward the wrongdoers, or take the surplus and what is easy of their charity (*ṣadaqāt*), and that was before the obligation of *zakāh* (obligatory almsgiving). (p-47) ﴿And enjoin what is known﴾, *al-maʿrūf* being what is recognized as good among actions. ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, so do not argue with them, nor repay them with the like of their actions. This verse comprises the noble qualities of character, commanding the Messenger to embody them.

﴿And if an incitement from Satan incites you﴾, meaning he prods you, *nakhs* being a prod, that is, a whisper that moves you to act contrary to what you were commanded, such as the onset of anger and anxious thought. *Al-nazgh*, *al-nasgh* and *al-nakhs* all mean piercing. He likened his whispering to people, inciting them to sins and agitating them, to the goad of a driver urging on what he drives. ﴿So seek refuge in Allah; indeed He is All-Hearing﴾, who hears your seeking refuge. ﴿All-Knowing﴾, who knows what is good for your affair so that He directs you to it. Or it means: All-Hearing of the words of whoever harms you, All-Knowing of his deeds, so He will recompense him for them, making you independent of retaliation and of siding with Satan.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 201–202:

﴿Indeed, those who have taquwa (God-consciousness), when a visitation (ṭā'if) from Satan touches them﴾ — a lamma (a passing whisper) from Him. It is an active participle from ṭāfa, yaṭūfu, as if it (the visitation) had circled around them and wheeled about them, so that it could not affect them. Or it is from ṭāfa bihi al-khayālu, yuṭīfu ṭayfan (the image, or phantasm, passed by him). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿ṭayfun﴾ (with a fixed vowel), either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as a lightened form of ṭayyif, like layyin and hayyin. By "Satan" is meant the species (al-jins), and that is why its pronoun is in the plural. ﴿They remember﴾ what God has commanded and forbidden. ﴿Then they see clearly﴾: by means of that remembrance, they perceive the places of error and the snares of Satan, so they guard against them and do not follow him in them. This verse is an emphasis and confirmation of what precedes it.

Likewise His words:

﴿But their brothers (the devils' brothers) pull them further﴾, i.e., and the brothers of the devils, those who have not had taqwa, by their extension (madd) of the devils, ﴿into error (al-ghayy)﴾, by adorning it for them and driving them towards it. It is also read as yamdūnahum, from amadda, and as yumādūnahum, as if they (the devils) help them through facilitation and incitement, while these (the unbelievers) help them by following and obeying. ﴿Then they do not hold back﴾: then they do not desist from misleading them until they bring them to ruin. It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the brothers, meaning they do not refrain from error and do not hold back as the God-conscious do. It is also permissible that by "the brothers" the devils are meant, and the pronoun returns to the ignorant (al-jāhilīn), so the statement runs in accordance with what it is about.

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign,﴾ from the Qur'an or from what they have proposed. ﴿they say, "Why do you not choose it?"﴾ That is, "Why do you not gather it (i.e., compose it) as a fabrication from yourself, like the rest of what you recite, or why do you not request it from Allah?" ﴿Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾ That is, I am not one who invents the signs, or I am not one who proposes them. ﴿These are insights from your Lord﴾ — this Qur'an is insights for hearts, by which the truth is seen and right judgment is grasped. ﴿and a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe﴾ — its explanation has already passed.

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ It was revealed concerning prayer: they used to speak during it, so they were commanded to listen to the recitation of the imam and to be silent for him. The apparent wording requires that both be obligatory wherever the Qur'an is recited in general, but the majority of scholars hold that both are recommended outside prayer. Whoever does not regard recitation as obligatory for the follower (ma'mum) has used this verse as evidence, and that argument is weak.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 205–206:

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾ is general to the remembrances (adhkar), including recitation (qira'ah), supplication (du'a') and others. Or it is a command to the follower (ma'mum, the one praying behind an imam) to recite silently after the imam has finished his recitation, as is the position (madhhab) of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. ﴿with humility and fear﴾ meaning humbly (mutadarri'an) and fearfully (khA'ifan).

﴿And without loudness in speech﴾ meaning speaking words that are above a whisper but below being loud, for this is more conducive to humility (khushu') and sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿in the mornings and evenings﴾ meaning at the times of morning (ghuduw) and the evenings (ashiyy). It is also read as "wal-aysal", which is a verbal noun of "asala", meaning he entered the time of asil (late afternoon), and it corresponds to "ghuduw". ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ of the remembrance of Allah.

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ refers to the angels of the exalted assembly (al-mala' al-a'la). ﴿do not disdain from His worship﴾ and they glorify Him and declare Him free of imperfection. ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾ and they single Him out for worship and humility, not associating anyone else with Him. This is an allusion to those among the accountable (mukallafin) other than them, and for this reason the prostration (sajdah, the prostration of recitation) was prescribed upon its recitation.

And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the son of Adam recites a prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping and says: 'Woe to him! This one was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so he has Paradise; and I was commanded to prostrate and I disobeyed, so I have the Fire.'" And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-A'raf, Allah will place between him and Iblis on the Day of Resurrection a veil, and Adam will be his intercessor on the Day of Resurrection."
